Katalog Berita (Halaman 54/57)

#741. Leading Cyber Expert: “We Are Entering the Flickers”

Former Defense Department Cyber Czar Brett J. Goldstein says Hollywood and media are about to get pummeled along with everyone else.

One hallmark of living in late-stage 2026 is the possibility that we’ll wake up and the news site we visit is down, or trying to steal our money. If we muster the courage to get out of bed, we shouldn’t expect to talk to anyone or go anywhere, as chances are that Outlook is offline or the FAA has grounded flights.Perhaps a bleak portrait, but one that has been painted in the past week with a host of cyber-security fails — “an advent calendar of societal collapse,” as Jon Stewart put it on The Daily Show Monday night. A slew of those fails have affected the media and entertainment worlds already, with CNN part of said crypto-swipe Tuesday morning and plenty of executives and workers stuck on the ground Friday. So far cyber experts don’t believe anything coordinated is happening here, even if some cable-news figures aren’t so sure. But even without a single unifying bad actor, the picture is bleak. Fading infrastructure combined with new AI tools that can easily exploit it can only spell trouble.For an industry still scarred by the 2014 Sony hack and all it exposed, the news hits hard. And Hollywood conducts a lot more business digitally these days than it did then, from all the Fandango ticket-ordering to the Spotify-streaming to the Disney+-subscribing. Cyber attacks and a faulty Internet hold the possibility of a major industry disruption. So how worried should the business — and we as individuals — actually be?For that we called Brett J. Goldstein. Goldstein (no relation to the Richmond barker, oi) holds an esteemed perch in American cyber defense, having occupied the role of director of the Defense Digital Service in the DoD under late-era Trump I and early Biden. He’s also a former Chief Information Officer for the city of Chicago and currently holds a professorship at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, where he runs a lab examining such threats. We caught up with him by Signal Tuesday.For anyone looking at all the failures and groundings in the past week, it can be hard not to connect the dots. Do you see them as related in any way or the result of one actor?I don’t know that there’s reason to believe its coordinated but it’s certainly a scary sequence of events which is very troubling. The loss of email or problems with Chase or groundings at United — just because it’s not coordinated doesn’t mean it’s not a cumulative problem.What are the roots of that problem in your view?What we are seeing is an under-investment in our infrastructure that is coming home to roost. You used to be able to hide — it used to take a determined researcher to find a security weakness. But now thanks to AI we can’t really hide. AI can find a needle in a haystack as never before. And so we have weaknesses as never before. Just look at PHP (a failure in Internet code baked-in during the 1990s that has been unearthed by AI). So we have to start fixing all of it, and we can’t put it off even one day.It feels like we have spent decades eating poorly and now, facing a potential heart attack, we’re trying to avoid it with a crash diet. Is this possible to fix quickly?I don’t know that it’s impossible but it’s certainly true we have a lot of sins to pay for. We need to pay our tech debt. There really are only two scenarios: the next few years will be either bumpy or really freaking bad. Everyone needs to change the way they’re thinking to make sure it’s the first one.So a best-case scenario is bumpiness. What does that look like?I think we are entering a period of the flickers and I think this past week has really demonstrated that. My sense is this is the beginning.You wrote in a Washington Post op-ed last week about those flickers. “For you, it looks like this. Your bank’s app is down. The pharmacy cannot pull up your prescription. Your paycheck is late — not stolen, just late because the payroll company unplugged its system to be safe. None of it is a catastrophe on its own. All of it, every week, is a different country from the one we live in now.”That is what will happen and all we can do is start fixing things across various sectors to shorten the period it happens. And [AI] frontier labs need to be a part of the solution too. If we bring quality [solutions] and stability we can make it less bumpy. But I don’t think we can avoid that we are entering the flickers. So we just need to start updating our systems.What does that mean for individuals? This feels like good advice if you run an IT department but what about as consumers? Signal over text, obviously. But what about everything else? Is clicking on CNN actually bad? Is my credit card exposed just because it’s on file at Hulu? Should we all just be moving to clay tablets?I would just say do all the things you’re supposed to do and don’t put it off. If a Chrome update button pops up for the love of Job click the freaking button. If there’s a patch, install it. Two-factor authentication and strong passwords and passkeys of course. If there’s something more complicated in your life consult a cyber expert. You need to do all of the steps, not some of the steps, not most of the steps. Noting is foolproof but there are ways to protect yourself more.Many people in the entertainment industry are especially worried because they still feel the aftereffects of the Sony hack. I talked to someone recently who was exposed and the way they spoke can only be described as a kind of PTSD. How likely is something on that scale happening again?I think there’s a lot of variance in the media sector just like there is in all sectors. Some companies and some individuals are reasonably protected and vigilant. And then with others it’s like “Oh my God, you’re so high profile and you’re not taking care of business.” But if the question is it more likely or less likely, of course it’s more likely. A few years ago when you thought about [a hack] it needed to be an adversary with a lot of tenacity and effort. Now AI-enabled scenarios make it so someone with no scruples can, without much effort, look at 100 things at once.The business side of Hollywood seems at risk as well. Streaming services rely on smooth digital interactions to conduct business; even a few seconds is critical, never mind compromised data or a daylong outage. How vulnerable are all those platforms?This is super-impactful for commerce. My core point if you’re in a position to do something at an organization is to set priorities. Yes you can do all the fancy front-facing AI stuff you’re doing but if you’re not doing the other stuff — if you’re not making sure the underlying platform is fundamentally sound and sustainable — none of that matters.OK, I’ve been putting it off. You’ve gotten into the bumpy scenario. What’s the really freaking bad one?Well, I’ll just say your whole day is tied to a system, and what happens if that system starts to unravel? If you can’t trust it? If it’s not just about a grounded flight which forces you to drive but everything else? But again, it’s an inflection point for us as a society. It’s not too late. We do have a choice.

#740. Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

Crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen. In experiments involving two carrion crows, the birds needed an average of just 235 milliseconds to determine which way a pattern of moving dots was traveling and respond with their choice. Despite their remarkable speed, they remained highly accurate.

The findings, published in the journal Science, offer new insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions. Researchers Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder from the University of Tübingen's Institute of Neurobiology found that the crows' rapid responses were accompanied by equally impressive activity in their brain cells.

Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy

To test the birds' decision-making abilities, the researchers presented them with moving dots on a touchscreen. The crows had to determine whether most of the dots were traveling left or right, then indicate their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen.

The birds performed remarkably well, even when the direction of movement was difficult to identify. "Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows' decisions were still better than random choices," Philipp Schmidbauer reports, "and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent."

The results showed that crows could evaluate visual information and make accurate choices in a fraction of a second. To understand how their brains accomplished this, the researchers examined the activity of individual neurons as the birds completed the task.

Crow Brains Begin Processing Decisions in Just 70 Milliseconds

The team recorded neural activity in a part of the bird brain called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This region plays an important role in processing information and making decisions, much like the prefrontal cortex in the human brain.

The recordings revealed that the crows' brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions almost immediately. Just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared, neurons associated with the different choices were already showing distinct patterns of activity.

These signals emerged well before the birds physically responded. As the crows evaluated the moving dots, neural activity steadily increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. The activity reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the bird ultimately selected.

Different Brain Structures, Similar Decision-Making Processes

One of the most intriguing findings is that crows appear to make decisions using neural processes similar to those found in humans and other primates, even though their brains are organized very differently.

"These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates," says Andreas Nieder.

Unlike mammals, birds do not have a cerebral cortex organized into layers. Nevertheless, their brains appear capable of following the same fundamental principles for evaluating evidence and reaching decisions. In this visual task, the crows completed that process twice as quickly as primates.

The researchers suggest that this exceptional speed could reflect the demands birds have faced throughout their evolution. Rapidly interpreting visual information and responding with precise movements are especially important for animals that fly and use their beaks to interact with their surroundings.

"Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging," Nieder explains.

However, the exact biological mechanisms responsible for the crows' speed advantage remain unknown. Further studies will be needed to determine how their differently structured brains can make comparable visual decisions so much faster than those of humans and monkeys.

#739. ‘Dancing With the Stars’: All 34 Winners

A Tony winner, several Olympians, Super Bowl champions, Bachelorettes and the Irwin siblings are just a few of the stars who have won the coveted mirrorball trophy throughout the show’s 20-year history.

It’s been two decades since Dancing With the Stars crowned its first winner. What started as a family-friendly dance competition show for a unique pool of celebrities has transformed into a cultural phenomenon.

Far before TikTok caught on to the merit the reality television series offers, ABC has been crowning winners of the show year after year. Dancing With the Stars has attracted quite an impressive slate of stars throughout its tenure, and a select few of them (34, to be exact) have snatched that mirrorball trophy and earned the coveted title of “winner.”

To celebrate the success of the series and commemorate its various champions who were crowned before the series earned its newfound virality, The Hollywood Reporter has rounded up all 34 winners of Dancing With the Stars.

This story was originally published in November 2025, and is updated as new winners are announced.

Kelly Monaco won the inaugural season of DWTS in 2005 alongside pro dancer Alec Mazo. That was far from the last time the General Hospital actress would be seen in the ballroom, as she notably competed on the 15th season with Valentin Chmerkovskiy as her partner.

Her double spin as a contestant on the series makes her one of six winners to return to the show to compete for a second time. She also appeared on season 25 to perform a trio number with Terrell Owens and Cheryl Burke, alongside six other former competitors.

Drew Lachey, former member of 98 Degrees and brother to Love Is Blind host Nick Lachey, picked up his mirrorball during season two. Partnered with Cheryl Burke, he returned for season 15 where he competed with Anna Trebunskaya.

Despite being named the show’s champion on his first DWTS turn, he was eliminated during week three during his second shot. However, Lachey, alongside Monaco, is still penned in the DWTS history books as one of the few winners to compete on the show more than once.

Cheryl Burke extended her winning streak into season three with Emmitt Smith. The former Dallas Cowboys running back made history with his 2006 win as the first (of four) NFL players to win DWTS. Plus, Smith is a part of the hexad of past champions who returned for season 15, where he was partnered with Cheryl once more.

Olympian Apolo Anton Ohno won the fourth DWTS installment, notably earning current co-host Julianne Hough her first mirrorball. Plus, Julianne’s season four victory also set the record for the youngest pro dancer to reign supreme, as she won the competition series at just 18 years old. (And she quickly made another record one year later.) Ohno also returned for season 15, and placed fifth.

Julianne Hough followed in Cheryl Burke’s footsteps in 2007 by winning the show for the second year in a row with racing driver Hélio Castroneves. The Indy 500 racer came back to DWTS in 2015 for season 15, where he placed 10th.

Olympic champion figure skater Kristi Yamaguchi translated her gold-medal winning talents into the DWTS ballroom in 2008, where she won season six. Her triumph saw Mark Ballas earn his first win as a pro dancer, one of many more to come.

Brooke Burke and current judge Derek Hough won the show’s seventh installment, which led to years of them both being intertwined with the DWTS family. Coming onto the show as a model and TV host, Burke offered the latter talent to the series as a DWTS co-host from season 10-17.

Brooke’s win was also served as Derek’s first win. While this list is intended to highlight the winners of the show, it’s also important to note that each celebrity victory also parlayed into the careers of the pro dancers that make up the series.

Shawn Johnson became the first gymnast to win DWTS in 2009. Partnered with Mark Ballas (marking his second victory), the gold medalist reappeared on the series for (you guessed it!) season 15 alongside Derek Hough.

Donny & Marie star Donny Osmond took his turn on the competition ballroom dance series in 2009, where he won season nine alongside Kym Johnson. He is notably the oldest person to ever win the show, as he was 51 at the time he was crowned champion.

Before Nicole Scherzinger won her Tony Award, she reigned victorious on DWTS. The former Pussycat Dolls singer was partnered with Derek Hough for the landmark 10th season.

Derek Hough won his fourth DWTS installment during season 11, with Dirty Dancing actress Jennifer Grey. Her first dance paid tribute to the film, a Viennese waltz set to “These Arms of Mine” by Otis Redding from the movie.

Grey long held the record for the most perfect scores in a season, setting it initially with six. She stands as the eldest woman to win DWTS, and she was 50 when she secured the title.

Former Pittsburgh Steelers player Hines Ward nabbed the DWTS season 12 champion title in 2012 with Kym Johnson.

Actor and Army veteran J.R. Martinez won season 13 alongside pro Karina Smirnoff, marking her first DWTS win. Following his victory, Martinez told The Hollywood Reporter he was “so grateful that I was able to be part of the journey to help get her first mirrorball trophy.”

Donald Driver, a former Green Bay Packers player, and Peta Murgatroyd won season 14 of DWTS. Following the triumph, he reflected on becoming another NFL star to win the mirrorball with THR.

“It took me 13 years to win the Super Bowl,” Driver joked. “I’m just glad it took me one season to win the mirrorball.”

The coveted 15th season of the show, better known as DWTS: All-Stars, was ultimately won by Melissa Rycroft. She was a contestant on The Bachelor season 13, and got engaged to Jason Mesnick, though he called off the engagement shortly after.

After her run as a Bachelor Nation star, she quickly pivoted to appearing on DWTS for season eight. (It’s a trend that would later catch wind for contestants in the franchise to go on the competitive dance show directly after their time searching for love on TV.) There, she placed third, before returning for season 15 and winning the mirrorball alongside Tony Dovolani.

American Idol alum Kellie Pickler returned to the competitive reality TV circuit in 2013, earning first place on season 16 of DWTS. She was partnered with Derek Hough, and notably beat out Zendaya for the top spot in the competition.

Marking the second time Derek Hough won consecutive seasons, Amber Riley was the show’s 17th winner. The Glee star and Derek had quite the impressive turn, tying the then-record for the highest first week score, receiving three nines from the judges. In total, she had five perfect scores throughout the season, which led her to nab the season 17 champion title.

Riley is also notably the first African American woman to win a regular, mainstay season of DWTS. (Melissa Rycroft won All-Stars.)

Olympic silver medalist Meryl Davis nabbed the DWTS mirrorball in 2014 alongside Makism Chmerkovskiy. She notably competed against her ice skating partner Charlie White, who placed fifth. At the time, she broke the record for the most perfect scored dances, with six.

Long before he became a co-host of DWTS, Alfonso Ribeiro won the show in 2014. Earning Witney Carson her first mirrorball as well, the duo were a force during the 19th installment. He matched Amber Riley’s record for best first week score ever, after earning 36/40 (meaning he received four nines from each judge).

Rumer Willis won the landmark 20th season of the competitive ballroom show alongside Valentin Chmerkovskiy, in his first win ever. Daughter to Demi Moore and Bruce Willis, Rumer matched Meryl Davis’ score of most perfect dances by a competitor.

One of the most heartwrenching journeys on DWTS came with Bindi Irwin’s season 21 appearance with her partner Derek Hough. Son of the beloved Steve Irwin, Bindi was the first winner to completely blow out the once-set record of most perfect dances. Jennifer Grey and Rumer Willis each had six, though Bindi earned eight perfect scores.

During Most Memorable Year week, she paid tribute to her late father with a touching contemporary that is ingrained in DWTS history. Competing on the show in 2015, her younger brother Robert Irwin later joined the show, partaking in season 34 of the series in 2025, exactly 10 years post-her tenure in the competition. After his win, they became the first sibling duo to both win DWTS.

Nyle DiMarco had a historic run during season 22 of DWTS, becoming the first deaf person to win the series. Hailing from one of the final cycles of America’s Next Top Model, DiMarco and Peta Murgatroyd’s time on the competitive reality show broke down barriers.

Another gymnast to be crowned a mirrorball champion, Laurie Hernandez won season 23 with Valentin Chmerkovskiy. She is the youngest DWTS winner ever, as she won the show when she was a mere 16-years-old in 2016.

Rashad Jennings is the fourth NFL player to win DWTS. He won with Emma Slater, marking her first and only win as a pro dancer in 2017.

Jordan Fisher and Lindsay Arnold won the show during 2017’s fall season. Fisher’s time on DWTS was record-breaking, as he notably earned nine perfect scores throughout season 25, taking over Bindi Irwin’s achievement of eight.

Olympic bronze medalist Adam Rippon won the first and only season of DWTS: Athletes. Sporting a cast of (you guessed it) only athletes, season 26 was a condensed, four-week installment that saw Jenna Johnson win her first mirrorball.

Bobby Bones’ DWTS win is one of the most controversial conquests in the show’s 20 year run. Dancing with his partner Sharna Burgess, the radio host had the lowest judges scores of the finalists during season 27. His win caused a shift in the DWTS universe — one that signified that viewers’ votes could successfully influence a celebrity to win a show without having the scoring to back it up.

Hannah Brown became the second Bachelorette to appear on DWTS during season 28, and the first to win, with her partner Alan Bersten, marking his first and only win.

Following directly behind her fellow franchise leader, Kaitlyn Bristowe won DWTS during the show’s first season set in the middle of the COVID-19 pandemic. In the fall of 2020, Bristowe earned the title of being the second Bachelorette to earn the mirrorball with her partner Artem Chigvintsev.

Iman Shumpert reigned supreme during another milestone season of DWTS. On season 30, he earned the title of the first NBA star to win the show, also earning Daniella Karagach’s first mirrorball.

Longtime DWTS champion pro Mark Ballas made his grand return to the ballroom after six installments off for an impressive season-long run with Charli D’Amelio. The first TikTok star to join the franchise’s cast, Charli earned six perfect scores during her run on the show. She is also a part of the first duo of non-spousal family members to compete on DWTS, as her mother, Heidi D’Amelio, also appeared on season 31.

Xochitl Gomez won the mirrorball trophy in the fall of 2023. She was partnered with Valentin Chmerkovskiy, notably standing as one of the youngest winners of the show, as she was 17 when she snatched the title.

Joey Graziadei is the most recent winner of DWTS, and the only Bachelor to ever win the competitive ballroom series. He was partnered with Jenna Johnson, totaling her number of wins up to two.

Robert Irwin and Witney Carson won the coveted mirrorball of DWTS‘ 2025 installment, putting a cap on one of the show’s most popular seasons ever. Following in the footsteps of his sister, Robert’s win extended the Irwin family’s impact on the competitive ballroom dance series. Plus, they are the only pair of siblings to both win DWTS.

The winner of Dancing With the Stars season 35 is soon-to-be-announced when the finale airs on Nov. 24. With the semi-final round of competition about to kick off, the champion will be one of the following celebrities still in the running: Tatyana Ali, Ezra Frech, Amber Glenn, Maura Higgins, Harry Shum Jr. or Connor Wood.

#738. 'It looked like every star in the sky was falling': Eyewitnesses remember the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966

It was a spectacle many regard as the greatest meteor display on record.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Overnight Nov. 17-18, 1966, the Leonid meteor storm thrilled stargazers during one extraordinary night when the stars themselves looked as though they were falling from the sky.

At the peak of the shower, observers at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona estimated an astonishing 40 meteors per second streaking across the sky. That's 2,400 shooting stars per minute, or a staggering 144,000 per hour. It was a spectacle that many regard as the greatest meteor display in recorded history.

It's hard to imagine what it was like to experience such a spectacle. But who better to tell us than those who saw it with their own eyes? To mark the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, we asked those who saw it to share their memories.

"I was around 9 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid storm, living a few miles east of Roxie, Mississippi. We lived in a rural, dark, relatively remote area with almost zero outside lights.

"I and a couple cousins were spending the night at our Uncle and Aunt's house, staying up late, just fooling around outside like young kids do when living in the 'sticks'. As we walked down a road, I remember hearing an almost constant series of little whistling, zipping sounds. The sounds were similar to when you light a nylon rope on fire and as it burns, little flaming droplets drip down with a zippy sound.

"I looked up and the sky was filled with streaks of 'shooting stars' and I realized that was what made the sounds. I yelled at my cousins to look up and we could hardly believe what we saw. We all laid down on our backs and for a couple of hours just watched and listened to what seemed like 1000's of 'shooting stars' zipping and zinging overhead. I could even smell the sulphur-like odor from the burning little bits of space dust.

"I'm nearly 70 years old now but I'll never forget that experience. I always knew what I'd seen that night was special but not until much later in life, after the internet, did I realize just how lucky I was to have experienced that storm. That night was one of the most loved and memorable nights of my life and I'll treasure it forever."

"I was an astronomy lab assistant at Southwestern College in Winfield, KS, in 1966, majoring in physics and math and the physics professor was sure that the Leonids would be an amazing shower worth the class time.

"The sky was clear. He called me early the morning of the 17th and told me to get to the campus. I can't remember the exact time as students and faculty were pounding on doors to get people, including neighbors,to watch.

"We were all lying in an open grassy area because that was the best way to see the whole sky. It was like a humongous fireworks display and lasted even as the sun began to rise.

"As years have gone by, I have felt grateful and privileged to have seen such a wonderful astronomical event."

"I was 18 and spent the night in El Paso, Texas, lying on the ground in my backyard and watching. It looked like every star in the sky was falling. It was amazing!"

"I was 9 years old and was camping with my dad in the western mountains of California. We were set up to sleep outside, but on this particular night, we saw more meteors than I have ever seen before or since. We watched them all night and didn't get much sleep."

"Brooklyn Center, Minnesota. 14 years old. Watched in our front yard. The sky was full. It took your breath away"

"I was 3 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid meteor shower. I remember very little at that age, but watching the sky fall that night was seared in my memory.

"My family was living in Troy, Alabama, at the time. My father, a professor of psychology, was a man of science with a special love of astronomy, which he passed onto his young son.

"He drove us several miles out of town until the skies were dark, without interference from the lights of the town. Troy was much smaller then and it was easy to find dark, clear skies.

"I remember that it was a little chilly that night. My father and I stretched out on the hood of the car, the warmth of the engine radiating against our backs.

"That night was my first meteor shower, and only many years later did I learn that year's Leonids were historic. Sadly, though I bore witness to the display, we missed the true event by several hours as I grew tired by 1:00 AM, and my father had to teach class in the morning.

"I remember many bright, colorful, and long-trailed meteors. Some left 'tails' that hung in the sky for several seconds. We only experienced the beginning of the event, but it is a core memory with my father.

"That night/morning spoiled me for future meteor watches; I assumed they would all be as interesting."

Not everyone was lucky enough to witness the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966. For some, the night was memorable for an entirely different reason.

Space.com columnist Joe Rao was just 10 years old at the time, and despite eagerly anticipating the display, the weather had other ideas.

"Standing in my backyard late on a Wednesday night in the Throggs Neck section of The Bronx, cursing the heavens. My grandfather stood at my side, just shaking his head and murmuring two words over and over: 'Too bad.'

"Clouds covered the midnight sky like a fresh coat of plaster, smearing my view of the Leonids. My mom, sister and grandmother, as well as my neighbors had long since trudged to bed, leaving only Grandpa and I to gaze at a charcoal gray sky totally devoid of stars."

Rao had been looking forward to the storm ever since a visit to New York's Hayden Planetarium, where astronomer Fred C. Hess had encouraged visitors to look out for what could be a spectacular display.

But when Rao and his grandfather ventured outside, there wasn't a single star in sight.

"After a few minutes, I sobbed to my grandfather, 'But they promised it was only going to be partly cloudy tonight.' To which he sadly replied, 'I guess the party is over.'"

The Leonid meteor shower occurs every November when Earth passes through a stream of debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years.

As tiny particles of comet dust enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of around 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up and produce brilliant streaks of light we know as meteors, or shooting stars.

Most years, the Leonids produce relatively modest displays with around 10 to 15 meteors per hour under ideal viewing conditions. But occasionally, Earth encounters a particularly dense trail of debris, triggering a meteor storm.

The Leonids have a long history of putting on some spectacular displays, with significant storms recorded in 1833 and 1866. And 1966 wasn't the last time the Leonids put on an extraordinary show. In 1999, 2001 and 2002, the Leonids once again reached meteor-storm levels, producing thousands of meteors per hour at their peaks. The shows aren't over yet! With comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle due to return in 2031, astronomers are already looking ahead to what the following years could bring.

A study released in August 2026 predicts potentially impressive Leonid displays in 2033 and 2034, with peak rates exceeding 1,000 meteors per hour. However, these forecasts remain uncertain, and a repeat of the extraordinary 1966 storm is far from guaranteed.

For now, we'll just have to wait and see.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

#737. Dark energy may have flipped from negative to positive 9.5 billion years ago

For decades, scientists have generally assumed that dark energy, the mysterious component thought to be responsible for the Universe's accelerating expansion, has remained constant throughout cosmic history. That long-standing assumption is now facing new scrutiny. Observations from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), which is constructing the largest three-dimensional map of the Universe, suggest that dark energy's influence may have changed over billions of years. Although the evidence is not yet strong enough to establish a discovery, it has renewed interest in a fundamental question: Could dark energy evolve rather than remain constant?

Researchers at Istanbul Technical University (ITU) have explored that possibility by taking a fresh look at an established alternative theory of gravity. In a 2025 study published in Physical Review D, an international team led by Prof. Özgür Akarsu of ITU's Department of Physics investigated a mathematical possibility that previous researchers had largely overlooked. Their analysis revealed a surprising scenario in which the effective density of dark energy was negative during the Universe's early history before eventually becoming positive.

The research was conducted within Akarsu's group at ITU, alongside postdoctoral researcher Dr. N. Merve Uzun and doctoral student Bilal Bulduk. The team also collaborated with Prof. Nihan Katırcı of Doğuş University, who previously worked as a postdoctoral researcher in Akarsu's group, and Prof. Antonio De Felice of Kyoto University's Yukawa Institute for Theoretical Physics, an internationally recognized center for theoretical physics.

An Overlooked Possibility in Einstein's Theory of Gravity

The discovery came from examining a part of an existing theory that had received relatively little attention. Rather than proposing an entirely new explanation for dark energy, the researchers revisited a framework known as teleparallel f(T) gravity.

Einstein's general theory of relativity explains gravity through the curvature of spacetime. Teleparallel gravity takes a different mathematical approach, describing gravity through a property called torsion. Scientists have spent years studying modified versions of this framework to investigate whether gravity itself might account for the Universe's accelerating expansion.

Earlier investigations of an exponential form of teleparallel gravity had concentrated on one particular set of mathematical solutions. This approach reflected a familiar assumption inherited from general relativity: dark energy should always have a positive density.

Akarsu and his colleagues decided to investigate what would happen if that restriction were removed. By considering a previously neglected branch of the theory, they uncovered a substantially different picture of how the Universe might have evolved.

Dark Energy May Have Switched From Negative to Positive

The team's calculations showed that two distinct cosmic histories could emerge even when the Universe contains the same amount of matter today.

One mathematical solution closely resembles the standard model of cosmology. The other predicts that effective dark energy had a negative density in the distant past. According to this second possibility, the density reached zero at approximately redshift 1.5, corresponding to roughly 9.5 billion years ago, before becoming positive and remaining that way.

What makes the result particularly interesting is that the researchers did not need to introduce an additional adjustable parameter to produce this behavior. Instead, the determining factor is related to the Universe's present matter density, which selects the mathematical branch. As a result, the model retains the same six cosmological parameters used in the standard ΛCDM model.

The theory also avoids an important potential problem. Although it predicts behavior that differs from Einstein's gravity across enormous cosmic distances, its departures from general relativity become naturally suppressed in dense environments. This allows the alternative solution to remain compatible with the highly accurate measurements of gravity made throughout the Solar System.

A Possible Explanation for the Hubble Tension

The new findings build on years of research into whether dark energy could have changed sign during the Universe's history.

Akarsu and his collaborators previously developed a framework called the sign-switching ΛCDM (ΛsCDM) model. In this scenario, the cosmological constant changes from negative to positive several billion years after the Big Bang.

Previous analyses found that a change in the sign of dark energy's density could agree with DESI observations while potentially reducing several unresolved disagreements in cosmology. One of the most significant is the Hubble tension, the persistent discrepancy between different methods of measuring the Universe's present expansion rate.

However, an important question remained unanswered. What underlying physical process could cause dark energy to undergo such a reversal?

The latest research offers a possible mechanism. Instead of requiring scientists to prescribe a sign change as part of the model, the reversal arises naturally from the mathematical structure of the modified gravity theory.

Akarsu explained why investigating an overlooked solution proved so valuable.

"For several years we have been studying a scenario in which dark energy switches sign, and it has held up remarkably well against data such as DESI's. The open question was what physical mechanism could produce such behavior. So we deliberately looked at a branch of a well-known theory of gravity that had been set aside because it violates the usual expectation that the dark energy density stays positive. The sign change emerged naturally from the theory itself."

DESI Observations Raise New Questions About Dark Energy

The theoretical findings have become especially relevant as astronomers gather increasingly detailed measurements of cosmic expansion.

DESI tracks the locations of millions of galaxies and quasars, allowing researchers to reconstruct how the Universe has expanded across billions of years. In March 2025, the DESI collaboration released findings based on its first three years of observations.

When combined with measurements of the cosmic microwave background, supernovae, and weak gravitational lensing, the results strengthened earlier indications that dark energy might not behave like a fixed cosmological constant.

These findings do not yet establish that dark energy changes over time. The statistical significance depends on which observational datasets are combined, and the evidence remains below the threshold required to claim a definitive discovery. Nevertheless, the possibility has motivated scientists to investigate alternative descriptions of cosmic expansion.

DESI has now completed its planned five-year survey, observing more than 47 million galaxies and quasars. The complete dataset will provide an even more demanding test of whether the apparent changes in dark energy persist as measurements become more precise.

The timing is also noteworthy. The ITU-led team's research was initially submitted in October 2024, several months before DESI announced its March 2025 findings. The researchers have not yet tested their model against the complete DESI dataset, making that comparison an important next step.

Could the Universe's Accelerating Expansion Be Slowing?

The significance of the proposed model extends beyond its prediction that dark energy's density may have changed sign.

Because the alternative solution emerges from a specific theory of gravity, it makes predictions about both cosmic expansion and how gravity behaves across the Universe. These predictions give astronomers ways to investigate whether the proposed cosmic history is consistent with observations.

Measurements of how galaxies and larger structures form and grow will be particularly important. Researchers can also examine how gravity bends light and how the Universe's expansion has changed over time. Among the most useful observational tests are structure growth, redshift-space distortions, and weak gravitational lensing.

Although comprehensive testing remains necessary, the initial results offer reasons for further investigation.

In an extended version of the theory that includes a cosmological constant, the researchers found that the model could remain consistent with observations of the cosmic microwave background while allowing the higher present-day expansion rates obtained from local measurements. This makes it a potentially useful approach to understanding the Hubble tension.

The extended model also permits another intriguing possibility: the acceleration of the Universe's expansion could have weakened or even stopped in the relatively recent cosmic past. Recent studies examining DESI observations have raised similar questions about whether cosmic acceleration has remained steady.

Importantly, neither the proposed dark energy reversal nor a recent slowdown in cosmic acceleration has been established as an observational fact. Both remain possibilities that must be tested against increasingly precise data.

Revisiting Gravity Could Reveal a Different Cosmic History

The research highlights how familiar scientific theories can contain possibilities that were missed because earlier investigations relied on restrictive assumptions.

In this case, allowing effective dark energy to have a negative density exposed an alternative evolutionary history within an already established mathematical framework. The researchers suggest that examining similarly overlooked solutions in other modified gravity theories could lead to additional insights.

Ultimately, the strength of the new explanation will depend on how well it reproduces the Universe astronomers actually observe. The full DESI dataset and other cosmological measurements will help determine whether this unusual version of cosmic history deserves a place alongside established explanations.

"We identified an alternative path for the Universe within an existing theory. The next step is to test it rigorously against the full observational data. The preliminary picture is encouraging, and we are particularly interested in what it may tell us about the Hubble tension," said Prof. Özgür Akarsu.

#736. Jeff Bezos Says He Was “Heavily Involved” in Casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond

The Amazon founder told a conference Tuesday that he and the film leadership were initially biased against Pattinson before realizing they found their man.

The names Bezos, Jeff Bezos. And he just chose the next James Bond.

The Amazon founder and chairman told a conference Tuesday that he “was heavily involved” in selecting Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond, working alongside the Amazon MGM leadership team, producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman, and director Denis Villeneuve.

“We ran a really tight process, and we made the final decision on Friday,” Bezos said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference. “There were a big group initially, and we selected down to five finalists, and then we did real old-fashioned screen tests of those five finalists.”

By now, those finalists are well known: Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden, Nicholas Hoult, and Pattinson, the man who ultimately secured Bond’s tuxedo.

Bezos says that they ran an elaborate screen test, with each actor performing three scenes with full costumes and sets.

“They were all amazing, but there was something special about Rob and his performances, and it was kind of immediately un-debated. Denis, the director was, we all sort of gravitated to him,” Bezos recalled. “By the way, initially, I would say we were slightly biased a little against him just because he’s already so famous. We sort of thought, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown. But in the screening tests, it was so obvious: He is James Bond.”

The casting of Pattinson is without question the biggest move yet by Amazon since it acquired MGM and since it bought out the Broccoli family for control of the franchise.

The irony is not lost on people that the Bond franchise is filled with tech tycoons and media industrialists as villains, from Hugo Drax in Moonraker to Max Zorin in A View to a Kill to Elliot Carver in Tomorrow Never Dies.

Now James Bond is firmly controlled by one of the world’s richest man, and a mogul whose empire spans tech, media, entertainment and even rockets into space. And this time he was the one helping to call the shots.

#733. The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse

In May 2024, an extraordinary solar storm sent brilliant auroras across skies in parts of the world where the northern and southern lights are rarely visible. But the spectacular displays were only the most obvious signs of an enormous disturbance unfolding in space around Earth. Deep within the planet's magnetosphere, the vast region controlled by its magnetic field, scientists were witnessing something they had never directly measured before.

The event began when a large sunspot unleashed several powerful solar eruptions in rapid succession. As enormous clouds of magnetized plasma raced through space, they combined before slamming into Earth's magnetosphere. The resulting storm produced the strongest magnetic disturbance ever measured in Earth's ring current, a vast region of electrically charged particles surrounding the planet.

For decades, researchers have debated where the particles that make up this ring current come from. Two major sources are known: the solar wind, which carries charged particles outward from the Sun, and Earth's ionosphere, an electrically charged layer of the upper atmosphere. Both typically supply particles during geomagnetic storms, and some scientists expected the solar wind to remain an important contributor during an extreme event involving particularly dense solar wind.

Instead, the first direct measurements of ring current composition during a storm of this magnitude revealed something remarkable. Particles originating from the solar wind contributed very little, while those coming from Earth's own atmosphere dominated to an extent never previously observed.

Published in Science Advances, the findings suggest that Earth's atmosphere may play a much greater role in determining the severity of extreme geomagnetic storms than scientists previously recognized. Because the dominant ions from Earth are much heavier than the particles supplied by the solar wind, they may have strengthened the magnetic disturbance and caused the ring current to reach its greatest intensity unusually close to the planet.

The discovery also strengthens the case for a proposed Japanese satellite mission designed to investigate how atmospheric particles enter space and influence powerful geomagnetic storms.

How the May 2024 Solar Superstorm Disrupted Earth's Magnetic Field

On May 10 and 11, 2024, enormous clouds of charged solar particles struck Earth's magnetosphere, triggering one of the most powerful geomagnetic storms in decades. Known as the "Gannon storm" or "Mother's Day storm," the event pushed the SYM-H index, a measure of geomagnetic disturbance, to a minimum of −518 nanotesla. This represented the second-largest recorded disturbance since 1981. The previous storm of comparable strength occurred in November 2004.

Although the colorful auroras drew worldwide attention, the consequences of such storms can extend far beyond the night sky.

"Some super or extreme geomagnetic storms are not just impressive light shows -- they pose radiation risks to spacecraft, disturb GPS signals and communications, and cause power outages. Understanding how a geomagnetic storm develops is not only a scientific question, but also one with real-world consequences," said Naritoshi Kitamura, lead author and designated assistant professor from the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research (ISEE) at Nagoya University.

A major source of these magnetic disturbances is Earth's ring current. This enormous belt of energetic charged particles, primarily oxygen and hydrogen ions, slowly circulates around the planet thousands of kilometers above the equator.

As the ions move, they create an electrical current that generates its own magnetic field. That field partly opposes Earth's natural magnetic field, weakening the magnetic field measured at ground level. The resulting changes are among the key signals scientists use to track the strength of geomagnetic storms.

Japanese Satellite Reveals an Unexpected Source of Storm Particles

Scientists were able to investigate the May 2024 storm in unusual detail thanks to Japan's Arase satellite, which was launched in 2016 and is operated by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). The ERG (Arase) science center is jointly operated by the Institute of Space and Astronautical Science (ISAS)/JAXA and the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research/Nagoya University.

Arase travels through the region of space where Earth's ring current forms. Its scientific instruments can measure both the mass and energy of individual ions, allowing researchers to determine the types of particles present during a storm.

By remarkable timing, the spacecraft passed through the ring current shortly after the May 2024 storm began and again as the disturbance approached its peak. These observations provided a rare opportunity to examine the composition of the ring current during an exceptionally powerful geomagnetic event.

"This is the first simultaneous observation of ring current ions and solar wind during a storm this large, and the data was clear -- approximately 85% of ions were oxygen from Earth's own ionosphere," Kitamura explained.

The overwhelming contribution from Earth's atmosphere was particularly surprising because the storm had been triggered by dense streams of material arriving from the Sun. Rather than supplying most of the ring current ions, the solar wind played a relatively minor role in the measured particle population.

The Arase measurements revealed another extraordinary feature of the storm. The magnetic field weakened dramatically in a region much closer to Earth than where similarly severe reductions had previously been documented.

"Near the peak of the storm, Arase detected a 40% decrease in magnetic field intensity at roughly 16,000 kilometers above Earth, and much closer to Earth than similar large decreases previously documented."

At the same time, the satellite detected a decline in the number of energetic electrons that normally circulate through this region of space.

Such an extreme weakening of the magnetic field can alter the paths followed by these electrons, causing them to drift away from their usual orbits. However, scientists have not yet determined whether the deformation of the magnetic field directly caused the observed electron loss. Further research will be needed to establish that connection.

Together, the observations provide new insight into how the ring current behaves during especially intense geomagnetic storms. They also suggest that the unusually large population of heavy ions originating from Earth's atmosphere may have helped produce the severe magnetic disturbance so close to the planet.

A New Clue to Predicting Dangerous Solar Storms

The findings could have important implications for space weather forecasting. Current models rely heavily on conditions in the solar wind to estimate how powerful an approaching geomagnetic storm might become.

However, the new measurements suggest that conditions within Earth's own upper atmosphere could also influence a storm's eventual intensity. Understanding how many atmospheric ions escape into the magnetosphere, and how they contribute to the ring current, may therefore be essential for making more reliable predictions.

The researchers believe that additional satellite observations could help answer these questions. Their findings support FACTORS, a proposed mission involving two satellites that is being prepared for an upcoming JAXA proposal opportunity.

FACTORS would investigate the processes that allow ions from Earth's atmosphere to flow into the magnetosphere and examine how those particles contribute to the development of geomagnetic storms.

By revealing how Earth's atmosphere and incoming solar material interact during extreme events, the mission could eventually improve forecasts of dangerous space weather. More accurate predictions would help scientists better anticipate storms capable of disrupting satellites, navigation systems, communications networks, and power infrastructure.

Materials provided by Nagoya University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

The International Documentary Association has revealed its nominees for the 2026 IDA Documentary Awards.

Concrete Land is the top nominee, up for six awards, including best feature documentary, followed by fellow best feature nominees To Hold a Mountain with five nods and A Fox Under a Pink Moon, Rehearsals for a Revolution and You Can See Everything with four nods each.

Astronauts get tasked with all kinds of weird science aboard the International Space Station. Recently, NASA astronaut and Crew-13 commander Jessica Watkins got to work supporting an ongoing experiment that includes 3D-printing human cells and tissues in space.

Aboard the space station, astronauts have a multitude of responsibilities ranging from station maintenance and repairs on spacewalks to daily exercise and a wide variety of scientific research.

Watkins recently shared a snapshot captured by her crewmate Anil Menon that showcases her experience working on an experiment called InSPA-Auxilium Bioprinter-Cell Printing that takes place inside the station's Life Sciences Glovebox, a contained research space and one of Watkins favorite places to work on the space station, she shared on social media.

In the image she is gloved-up with both her hands and arms covered in the sealed glovebox while she mixes samples of living cells with a bioink, a mixture she then inserts into a specialized cartridge, NASA shared.

This experiment that Watkins is working on "leverages the microgravity environment of ISS to 3D print cells and manufacture human liver, kidney, and cartilage tissue. Just one of many examples of how we’re using this amazing orbital national laboratory to reshape our understanding of biology, medicine, and engineering, and improve life on Earth!" Watkins shared online.

This experiment is designed to explore 3D printing human cartilage tissue in microgravity. The experiment aims to one day support future human patients both in space and on Earth.

When you think of the research that happens in space, 3D-printing human cells might not be the first thing to come to mind. But because of the unique microgravity environment onboard the ISS, it is the perfect home for even the strangest of biological experiments.

On the space station, there is still gravity but objects (and people) remain in a sort of constant freefall, leading to total weightlessness that mimics the complete absence of gravity. This weightlessness allows researchers to test, experiment and explore beyond the gravitational confines of Earth.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. You can follow her online @chelsea.gohd and @foxanne.music

#730. NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks

Organic carbon has been confirmed in two ancient Martian rocks examined by NASA's Perseverance rover, adding an important new piece to the puzzle of whether Mars once supported life. Even more surprising, the material was found just beneath the planet's surface, where harsh conditions can destroy organic compounds.

The discovery builds on NASA's September 2025 announcement that Perseverance had identified a potential biosignature. A potential biosignature is a substance or feature that could have formed through biological activity, although other explanations are possible. Now, research published in Science Advances provides definitive confirmation that the same two rocks, located in Mars' Bright Angel formation, contain organic carbon, an essential component of life. The findings also offer a clearer picture of the material's characteristics and how it may have been preserved.

The study was co-led by Ashley Murphy, a postdoctoral researcher at the Planetary Science Institute, and Kyle Uckert, Deputy Principal Investigator of the SHERLOC instrument.

NASA's Perseverance Rover Detects Complex Organic Carbon

To investigate the rocks, researchers used the Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman & Luminescence for Organics & Chemicals (SHERLOC) instrument mounted on Perseverance's robotic arm. The instrument examined several rocks in the Bright Angel formation within Jezero crater, where the rover also collected a sample from a rock named "Cheyava Falls."

SHERLOC uses a technique called Raman spectroscopy, which shines laser light onto a material to identify and map its minerals and organic compounds without damaging the rock.

The measurements revealed macromolecular carbon (MMC), a form of carbon consisting of large, interconnected networks of carbon atoms. This type of material is also found in rocks on Earth and in meteorites. Importantly, it can form through biological activity or through chemical processes that do not involve life, so its presence alone cannot establish that Mars was once inhabited.

The surrounding geology offers additional clues about how the material reached these rocks. Billions of years ago, water flowed through a river channel into Jezero crater, carrying sediment that gradually settled on the bottom. Over time, those fine particles hardened into the mudstone formations Perseverance is now exploring.

Researchers detected the carbon within these ancient sediments and alongside carbonate and sulfate minerals that developed later as water altered the rocks. This distribution raises the possibility that organic material entered or formed within the rocks during at least two separate periods of Mars' geological history.

"While the specific formation mechanism of the MMC detected in the Bright Angel mudstones remains unknown, this is still one of the most exciting findings to date," Murphy said.

Organic Carbon Survives Just Beneath Mars' Harsh Surface

One of the most striking results concerns where the organic carbon was found. The material survived only a few microns below the exposed Martian surface, at a depth smaller than the thickness of a sheet of paper. This is the shallowest detection of macromolecular carbon ever reported on Mars.

That location makes the finding particularly unusual. Mars' surface is exposed to radiation, sunlight, and chemically reactive substances that can break down organic molecules. Scientists would generally expect these conditions to make long-term preservation especially difficult so close to the surface.

"The Martian surface environment includes radiation and chemical oxidants that are destructive to organics, and terrestrial laboratory simulations have shown that the survival time of organics in Martian-like conditions -- especially at or near the surface -- depends on factors such as the type of organic molecule and the surrounding minerals," Murphy said. "The MMC detected in the Bright Angel mudstones is either resistant to degradation and/or has been sufficiently shielded by other minerals, such as clays, or iron-rich Martian soil."

In other words, the carbon may have survived because of its own chemical durability, protection provided by surrounding minerals, or a combination of the two. Understanding how it endured could help scientists determine where similar organic compounds might remain preserved elsewhere on Mars.

Ancient Martian Lakes and Rivers May Have Been Rich in Organic Material

The findings also suggest that organic carbon may not have been confined to a single region of ancient Mars.

Perseverance collected the Bright Angel sample more than 2,000 miles from Gale Crater, where NASA's Curiosity rover previously detected organic compounds. Finding organic material at such widely separated locations suggests that the chemistry associated with life's building blocks may once have been common across the Martian landscape.

"It is encouraging for Martian habitability," Murphy said. "This indicates that billions of years ago, organics may have been more than just locally present and may have been more widely available in ancient lakes and rivers on Mars."

The possibility of widespread organic material is significant because ancient Mars once had environments containing liquid water. If organic compounds were also broadly available, some of those lakes and rivers may have offered important chemical ingredients for life.

However, discovering those ingredients does not mean that living organisms were present. Organic carbon can be produced without biology, and scientists still need to determine exactly how the material in the Bright Angel rocks formed.

Could Martian Rocks Preserve Evidence of Ancient Life?

Determining whether the Bright Angel formation contains fossilized microorganisms remains beyond the capabilities of the rovers currently exploring Mars. Neither Curiosity in Gale Crater nor Perseverance in Jezero Crater carries the large, energy-intensive laboratory equipment needed to conclusively distinguish fossil evidence of ancient life from geological processes.

Perseverance was designed to search for potential biosignatures, including features like those identified in the Cheyava Falls rock. From that perspective, the discovery represents a "resounding win for Mars science," Murphy said.

The next major step would be to examine Martian samples using the more sophisticated instruments available in laboratories on Earth. Such equipment could reveal details too small or chemically subtle for the rover's instruments to resolve, helping researchers determine whether biological processes or nonliving chemistry produced the organic carbon.

If samples from the Bright Angel formation eventually reach Earth, scientists hope to study their minerals and organic compounds with much greater sensitivity and resolution. These investigations could help explain how the macromolecular carbon formed, how it survived, and what its presence reveals about the distribution of organic material across Mars.

Murphy continues to collaborate with the SHERLOC science team as Perseverance explores the Martian surface. Her research also includes studying Earth materials that resemble Martian rocks and using Raman spectroscopy to improve how scientists interpret the measurements returned by the rover.

Murphy's work on SHERLOC Instrument Mars 2020 was supported through JPL Subcontract No. 1641753 to the Planetary Science Institute.

#729. The Next Bond Villain: From Idris Elba to Kristen Stewart, 22 Actors Who Should Face Off Against Robert Pattinson

Every James Bond is only as good as the person who’s trying to kill him.

Throughout the franchise’s history, we’ve seen Sean Connery take on Gert Fröbe’s Goldfinger, Roger Moore tackle Christopher Walken’s Max Zorin and, in the Daniel Craig era, Mads Mikkelsen’s Le Chiffre in “Casino Royale” and Javier Bardem’s notorious Raoul Silva in “Skyfall.” In a Bond film, the movie cannot succeed without the diabolical plan and villain that’s trying to destroy the world or the shaken, not stirred man in the tux.

After the news that Robert Pattinson has been cast to portray the infamous hero in an upcoming film from Denis Villeneuve, the search is on for the next “Bond Girl” and now the anticipated adversary that threatens his mission to keep the world safe.

The wish list includes many familiar faces from Pattinson’s past, both in front and behind the camera and some long-shot selections that may be crazy enough to work. Whether it’s a tech messiah, a rogue spy or an heiress with a doomsday device, we’re excited.

Here are the 22 actors Variety would love to see go toe-to-toe with the new 007.

Honorable mentions: Mahershala Ali, Austin Butler, Cate Blanchett, Willem Dafoe, Mia Goth, Nicholas Hoult, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Wagner Moura, Dev Patel, Matthew Rhys, Callum Turner

Riz Ahmed is skilled in dramatic roles, like his Oscar-nominated performance as a troubled drummer in “Sound of Metal.” But he’s also a master of voice and motion-capture acting, from Severus Snape in the “Harry Potter” audiobooks to the ruthless symbiote leader Riot in “Venom.” So whether he plays it straight or perhaps takes the form of a monstrous menace to Robert Pattinson’s Bond, Ahmed has the subtle, steely power to be a baddie either way.

Pierce Brosnan led four James Bond films as the titular superspy in the late ’90s, so why not bring him home for one last ride as the silver-haired supervillain?

Brosnan, who was vocal throughout the 007 casting process, has remained a staple of the action genre 24 years after his final turn as Bond in “Die Another Day.” He recently lent his espionage expertise to Steven Soderbergh, playing the double-agent villain in his twisty spy thriller “Black Bag.” Also on the villain front, Bronsan has been stirring up trouble as the leader of the Irish mob in “Mobland,” which is wrapping its second season.

Director Denis Villeneuve is about to bring Timothée Chalamet through his villain arc in “Dune: Part Three,” and he may want to bring that tyrannical overlord energy with him to the Bond franchise. Chalamet, like Robert Pattinson, is one of Hollywood’s most in-demand stars, which makes him an intriguing on-screen rival. Chalamet has built his young career playing righteous leading men, however complicated they may be, in films like “Marty Supreme,” “A Complete Unknown” and “Wonka.” It could be time for Chalamet to stay on the dark side for a bit longer and take on cinema’s suavest spy.

If Pattinson made his case for playing Bond with Nolan’s time-bending spy thriller “Tenet,” then Debicki should also be strongly considered alongside him. The two of them had standout roles in the movie, and we’re dying for them to get some more screen time together. “He is an enigma himself,” Debicki told Variety about Pattinson’s Bond casting. “He’s beautiful, and he’s funny and he’s smart. I think he’s perfect. I’m so thrilled.”

Having spent so many years being tipped by the media for the 007 job — and then being asked about Bond in every interview — it feels only right that Idris Elba be given a juicy bad guy role to play. But this is no consolation prize for the Brit, who has excelled in intimidating, scene-commanding villainy on more than one occasion, including as the brooding and calculating Stringer Bell in his “The Wire” breakout, the ruthless mercenary leading a group of child soldiers in “Beasts of No Nation,” the genuine action movie baddie in “Hobbs & Shaw” and, er, the master criminal feline Macavity in “Cats.” OK, fine.

Colin Farrell has already gone toe-to-toe with Pattinson, buried under prosthetics as Oz Cobb in “The Batman.” The Oscar nominee from “The Banshees of Inisherin” has played a hit man with a conscience in films like “In Bruges” and an assassin as Bullseye in “Daredevil.”

Now let’s picture that Irish charm curdling into something far more dangerous, like an arms baron who’s a blast to watch even as he’s trying to kill Bond. Do it.

Fassbender spent years playing an empathetic villain in Fox’s “X-Men” series as a young Magneto. Now, he’s played a suave spy in last year’s surprise sleeper hit “Black Bag,” a cold assassin in David Fincher’s 2023 thriller “The Killer” and a CIA officer in “The Agency” on Paramount+. He certainly fits the bill to star in a Bond movie, perhaps as a double-crossing 00 spy who faces off against Pattinson.

Rebecca Ferguson has shown she can keep up with Tom Cruise’s Ethan Hunt in the “Mission: Impossible” franchise, so it could be time for her to face off against cinema’s other iconic man of mystery.

Outside of her three “Mission” films, she recently took on internal affairs as a high-level situation room officer in Kathryn Bigelow’s “House of Dynamite.” Ferguson is probably best known for her leading role in Apple TV’s “Silo” as Juliette Nichols, a mechanic-turned-post-apocalyptic liberator. It also helps she’s in Denis’ orbit already with the “Dune” franchise.

She’s already a pro at unraveling a conspiracy, so she is sure to be an expert at weaving one together in the face of Bond.

Walton Goggins is already one of Amazon’s most valuable assets, starring in Prime Video’s post-apocalyptic drama “Fallout” as a 200-year-old zombie cowboy.

Of course, Goggins made Boyd Crowder, the silver-tongued soul of FX’s crime drama “Justified,” one of his most memorable creations. Plus, he nearly stole the show on HBO’s anthology series “The White Lotus” as the haunted Rick.

Some of the best Bond villains are a little unhinged and completely charming, and Goggins brings both.

Villeneuve and Gyllenhaal have already worked together on “Prisoners” back in 2013, and they’re long overdue for a reunion. Gyllenhaal has played a wide variety of unsettling bad guys in recent years, like a grimy journalist in “Nightcrawler,” a theatrical Mysterio in “Spider-Man” and a smooth-talking criminal in “Ambulance.” He’s also bulked up and trained in UFC fighting for two “Road House” movies. His Bond villain could mix all of these past roles into one and be a true chameleon.

Isn’t it safe to say that AMC’s “The Night Manager” was pretty much Tom Hiddleston’s 007 audition tape?

He reprised his role as former British intelligence operative Jonathan Pine earlier this year in the second season streaming on Prime Video. However, the tuxedo never came, so maybe being another scene-stealing bad boy can get him into the fold. As Loki in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Hiddleston proved audiences will adore a villain even while he betrays everyone.

Maybe casting him as a disgraced MI6 golden boy, or an agent who was supposed to get the number but then didn’t, will let him spend the whole movie proving he actually deserved it.

Angelina Jolie has already shared the screen with one 007 when Daniel Craig played her rival in “Lara Croft: Tomb Raider” (2001). What if she took a shot at the next one?

The Oscar winner of “Girl, Interrupted” has played both sides of the spy game in films like “Salt” and “Mr. & Mrs. Smith.” She also gave Disney one of its most iconic villains in the live-action format with “Maleficent.”

Let her bring a menacing rage to the MI6 team and watch what happens.

Daniel Kaluuya is reuniting with his “Judas and the Black Messiah” director, Shaka King, on a new Amazon MGM movie, “The Parlay,” so technically he’s already in the family, right?

For anyone who saw Steve McQueen’s “Widows,” they’ll remember how terrifying the Oscar winner can be as he played the enforcer Jatemme and delivered one of the most chilling henchmen of the past decade. Let’s not forget “Black Panther,” where he played W’Kabi, the trusted friend who betrays his king.

Once thrown out as a worthy contender to play Bond, this Londoner, with his knack for exuding menace, would have MI6 very worried.

Barry Keoghan has already said that, rather than Bond, he’d prefer to play the villain. Still, he’s certainly got the credentials to prove it. From a sinister teen who embarks on a campaign of revenge in “The Killing of a Sacred Deer” to a swaggering, volatile gangster in “Calm with Horses” to the murderous manipulator of “Saltburn,” the Irishman has shown he could be 007’s perfect, cherubic master of menace. And then there’s that deleted scene in “The Batman” as the Joker opposite Pattinson. Time for a proper face-off between the two.

From Nolan to Villeneuve, Murphy could follow Robert Pattinson from one major director to another. Murphy hit the lotto with his “Oppenheimer” Oscar win, and playing a Bond villain could be his second wave. We know he’s up to the challenge after seeing him as J. Robert Oppenheimer, the Scarecrow in “Batman Begins” and Tommy Shelby in “Peaky Blinders.” Aside from a cameo in “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple,” Netflix’s “Peaky Blinders” movie and a return in “A Quiet Place 3,” Murphy’s slate has been too quiet since “Oppenheimer” and a Bond movie would be the perfect big-screen welcome back.

Upon learning that Pattinson would be Bond, Pitt pitched himself to play the villain at his “Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” premiere. Pitt has produced “Mickey 17” and “The Lost City of Z,” both of which starred Pattinson, so the two already have a connection. “I love what he’s been doing. I love his choices. I think he’s the real deal. That’s good. A good call, I like it,” Pitt said, then threw his hat in the ring to play the bad guy. “I’d like to do that. My man Javier [Bardem] did it so well. It’s tall shoes, but I’d take that on.”

Nobody in Hollywood makes politeness more terrifying than Jesse Plemons.

He was Todd, the soft-spoken killer of AMC’s crime series “Breaking Bad.” In Alex Garland’s “Civil War,” he turned one question, “What kind of American are you?“ into one of the frightening scenes of the year, in a one-scene wonder, no less.

A Bond villain who never raises his voice and never apologizes before he pulls the trigger. That’s what exactly Plemons does best.

The Oscar nominee of “The Power of the Dog,” who won Best Actor at Cannes for “Kinds of Kindness,” is playing Plutarch Heavensbee in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” this year, a role originated by the late Philip Seymour Hoffman. And famously, also played a villain in “Mission: Impossible III” (2006).

Florence Pugh may be on many fans’ lists as a potential Bond girl (and so did Variety), but it seems the Brit — who stars alongside Robert Pattinson in “Dune: Part Three” — would rather go a different route. Speaking at Elle’s Women in Hollywood event shortly after 007 was cast, she said she’d messaged Villeneuve to say: “Congratulations on finding your Bond, nice catch. Any villains the size of a 5ft 4in female?” While Pugh’s roles haven’t yet seen her dip into full-scale global terrorism, as Cathy in the recent “East of Eden” adaptation, she has shown she could certainly explore her darker side.

With his shape-shifting ability to transform into a menacing clown or a cadaverous vampire, Bill Skarsgård can become just about any villain the Bond creative team imagines.

Skarsgård’s roles in “It,” “Nosferatu,” “Barbarian,” and “The Crow” are just a few of the horror-tinged roles he’s inhabited, suggesting his take on a Bond villain could lean more toward the grotesquely menacing side. The Swedish actor even appeared with Robert Pattinson, a fellow famous vampire, in the Netflix movie “The Devil All the Time,” though they didn’t share any scenes.

As soon as Pattinson’s name was floated as 007, hordes of Twihards were immediately fan-casting Stewart to give the Bond universe a “Twilight” crossover. But instead of playing a Bond Girl, Stewart would be a much more entertaining choice as a villain. Please, Amazon MGM, make this ultimate Bella Swan and Edward Cullen fan fiction come true. Better yet, cast Taylor Lautner as a henchman to Stewart’s Bond villain.

A great James Bond villain is known for their striking, singular presence – and who better to provide that presence than Tilda Swinton? Her otherworldly, androgynous persona has been put to good use by everyone from the Avengers to Wes Anderson, Bong Joon Ho and the Coen brothers, and she could easily switch on the evil vibes as a Bond villain. Swinton hasn’t worked with Robert Pattinson yet, but Pattinson is a big admirer of her performance in 2008’s “Julia.” “I think that’s one of the great performances, and it’s kind of criminally underseen,” he told Rotten Tomatoes.

In “I’m Still Here,” Fernanda Torres played Eunice Paiva, a woman standing up to a military dictatorship and the role earned her a Golden Globe statue and an Oscar nomination for best actress. While on the awards circuit, the Brazilian star knew exactly what she wanted to do with her next big venture: play a Bond villain.

“I would love to be the secretary of a James Bond villain,” she said on the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast. “And just say, ‘He will be waiting for you in the next room, Mr. Bond.’ That’s it. That’s my dream. Just this line. That’s all I want to do.”

Imagine Torres as the power behind the throne: a Rio de Janeiro media baroness who smiles for the cameras while quietly buying off half the government?
