#728. Superheated magma could fuel towering lava fountains

Why do some volcanoes send towering fountains of lava into the sky while others release molten rock in much calmer eruptions? Scientists have discovered that a hidden effect of extreme heat inside magma may help explain these striking differences.

An international research team led by The University of Manchester investigated volcanic material from the 2021 Tajogaite eruption on La Palma, Spain. Their findings reveal that a process known as "superheating" can dramatically slow the formation of crystals inside magma as it travels upward toward Earth's surface.

Superheating occurs when magma reaches temperatures above those at which its crystals would normally remain stable. The researchers found that this extra heat can keep magma relatively fluid for much longer than expected, potentially allowing it to rise rapidly and produce spectacular lava fountains.

The discovery, published in Nature Communications, offers new insight into a long-standing question in volcanology: How does magma's temperature history influence the way a volcano erupts?

How Extreme Heat Changes Magma Deep Inside Volcanoes

Magma is a mixture of molten rock, gases, and sometimes solid crystals beneath Earth's surface. Once it emerges from a volcano, it is called lava. Although temperature and chemical composition are important in determining how magma behaves, the new research suggests that the heating it experienced before an eruption can also make a major difference.

Under normal conditions, crystals begin forming as magma cools. This process often starts around tiny existing crystals that act as "seeds," providing surfaces on which additional crystals can grow.

Superheating can disrupt this process in two important ways. First, sufficiently high temperatures can dissolve the microscopic crystal seeds that would otherwise encourage new crystals to develop. Second, the heat changes the internal structure of the molten material, making it more uniform and less favorable for new crystal formation.

These changes matter because crystals affect magma's viscosity, which describes how easily a substance flows. As more crystals develop, magma generally becomes thicker and more resistant to movement. This can influence both its speed of ascent and the way trapped volcanic gases escape.

Lead author Dr. Barbara Bonechi, Research Associate at The University of Manchester, explained:

"The history of crystal and bubble growth can dramatically control how a magma erupts, in particular as more crystals grow, they eventually have a dramatic effect on magma viscosity. Until now, we did not fully understand the dynamics of crystal growth for magmas that received an injection of superheat just before ascent. But using our exciting and newly developed X-ray transparent pressure vessel combined with synchrotron X-ray microtomography, we can actually observe these processes 'in situ'."

Scientists Discover an Eight-Hour Delay in Crystal Formation

To investigate what happens inside superheated magma, the researchers recreated volcanic conditions in the laboratory using material collected from the Tajogaite eruption. The magma involved in that eruption may have experienced superheating before reaching the surface and while rising through Earth's crust.

The team conducted experiments under carefully controlled temperatures and pressures designed to reproduce conditions encountered by magma underground.

At Diamond Light Source, a major scientific research facility, the researchers used synchrotron X-ray microtomography to watch crystals develop in real time. This advanced imaging technique uses extremely powerful X-rays to examine the internal structure of materials in three dimensions without having to cut them open.

A specially developed pressure vessel that allows X-rays to pass through it made these observations possible while the magma was subjected to volcanic conditions.

The team also performed complementary experiments in Prague, where samples could be examined over longer periods outside the real-time imaging setup. Together, these approaches allowed the researchers to observe how different heating conditions affected the timing of crystal formation.

The results revealed a remarkable difference.

Magma that had not undergone superheating began producing crystals after approximately 20 minutes. However, when magma was subjected to strong superheating, the beginning of crystallization was delayed for more than eight hours.

This substantial delay suggests that intense heating can leave magma without newly forming crystals for far longer than scientists might otherwise expect, with potentially important consequences for volcanic eruptions.

Why Superheated Magma Could Produce Towering Lava Fountains

The researchers next explored how these laboratory findings might affect real volcanoes.

They incorporated the measured delays in crystal formation into computer models that simulate how magma rises through Earth's crust. These models account for changes in magma properties as the molten material moves toward the surface.

The simulations revealed two very different possibilities.

When superheating delays crystallization, magma can remain relatively fluid as it rises. Because it encounters less resistance to flowing, it may travel upward more rapidly, potentially creating conditions that favor dramatic lava fountains.

These spectacular eruptions occur when escaping volcanic gases propel molten rock high above a vent, producing jets and fountains of glowing lava.

In contrast, magma that begins crystallizing earlier becomes more viscous and tends to ascend more slowly. This slower movement gives volcanic gases additional time to escape, favoring gentler eruptions in which lava flows out onto the surface rather than being thrown high into the air.

Such behavior is known as an effusive eruption, a type of volcanic activity characterized primarily by flowing lava.

The findings suggest that even when volcanic systems have similar characteristics, differences in their earlier heating histories may help explain why their eruptions look and behave so differently.

A New Clue for Predicting Volcanic Eruptions

Understanding what happens to magma before it reaches the surface is essential for assessing volcanic hazards. Scientists monitor signals such as earthquakes, ground deformation, and volcanic gas emissions to identify changes within active volcanoes.

However, predicting exactly how an eruption will unfold remains difficult. Two volcanoes with seemingly similar magma compositions and gas conditions can still display markedly different eruptive behavior.

The new research suggests that the effects of superheating and the timing of crystal formation deserve greater attention in volcanic forecasting models.

By accounting for these previously underappreciated processes, researchers may eventually be able to better interpret volcanic monitoring data and assess whether rising magma is more likely to produce vigorous lava fountains or gentler lava flows.

The results do not mean that magma temperature alone determines how explosive an eruption will be. Instead, they identify another important piece of the complex physical processes that shape volcanic activity.

Co-author Dr. Margherita Polacci, Senior Lecturer in Volcanology at The University of Manchester, highlighted the potential importance of the findings for understanding volcanic hazards:

"Current volcanic hazard models typically focus on magma chemistry, gas content and pressure changes. This work suggests that pre-eruptive thermal history and crystallization kinetics may also play an important role in controlling magma ascent and eruptive behavior, with implications for volcanic hazard assessment."

Voyager 1 has gone farther than any other object built by humanity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft prepares to reach a historic distance from Earth, the agency is inviting people around the world to celebrate by shining a light into the night sky in honor of humanity's farthest-flung spacecraft.

The event, called "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," will take place after sunset on Tuesday (Nov. 17), the day before Voyager 1 gets one light-day from Earth. And that's a big milestone: One light-day is the distance light travels in a day — about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers).

NASA is encouraging "Shine Bright" participants to create a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet by flashing the spacecraft's three-letter mission call sign, VGR, in Morse code, according to a statement from the space agency.

To celebrate the spacecraft, participants can use a flashlight, phone, bike light or other portable light source to send the signal skyward. And don't fret if you're unfamiliar with Morse code: NASA has created an automated flasher that can be opened in a smartphone or tablet browser to display the VGR sequence.

The spacecraft’s call sign pattern consists of three quick flashes followed by one long flash for the letter V, two long flashes and one quick flash for G, and one quick flash, one long flash and another quick flash for R. Participants are encouraged to repeat the sequence for about a minute, NASA officials said.

NASA also invites people to photograph or record their light signals and share them on social media, tagging the agency's official account, @NASA. The goal is to create a worldwide display of light marking a milestone nearly five decades in the making.

The celebration is intended as a symbolic tribute rather than an actual attempt to communicate with Voyager 1. At a distance of one light-day from Earth, the spacecraft is so far away that even radio signals traveling at the speed of light take approximately 24 hours to reach it. A flashlight or phone signal from Earth, of course, cannot reach the probe; NASA communicates with it using its Deep Space Network of radio dishes.

Launched on Sept. 5, 1977, Voyager 1 has spent nearly 50 years traveling through space and is now the most distant human-made object from Earth. When it reaches the one-light-day milestone, it will have traveled a distance that light itself takes 24 hours to cross. Its twin, Voyager 2, is expected to reach the same milestone in November 2035. (The two spacecraft took different routes through the solar system.)

The public celebration will be followed by another opportunity to learn more about the historic mission. On Thursday (Nov. 19) at 12 p.m. EST (1700 GMT), NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California will host a moderated discussion with Voyager mission team members and NASA leadership.

The discussion will cover the current status of both Voyager spacecraft, the unique scientific observations they continue to collect in interstellar space and the engineering challenges involved in keeping the nearly 50-year-old probes operational. A question-and-answer session with members of the media and audience will follow. NASA will also offer a preview of an upcoming Voyager documentary planned for release in 2027, coinciding with the mission's 50th anniversary.

For a mission that has carried humanity's message into interstellar space for nearly half a century, the "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day” offers a chance for people back on Earth to mark just how far these pioneering spacecraft have traveled. More details about NASA's automated VGR flasher and step-by-step Morse code instructions are available online.

#726. Marvel Started Planning for Robert Downey Jr.’s Doctor Doom Before Jonathan Majors Was Fired and ‘Avengers: The Kang Dynasty’ Fell Apart, Says Kevin Feige

Before “Avengers: Doomsday,” there was “Avengers: The Kang Dynasty.” Marvel Studios boss Kevin Feige announced the latter title at Comic-Con in July 2022, with Jonathan Majors’ Kang the Conqueror poised to become the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s next Thanos-sized villain starting with 2023’s “Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania.”

Those plans, however, were upended a few weeks after “Quantumania” opened in theaters and earned some of Marvel’s worst reviews and box office. Majors was arrested in March 2023 after he assaulted his then-girlfriend in the backseat of a private vehicle. The actor was officially convicted in December 2023, with a six-person jury finding him guilty of two misdemeanor counts of harassment and assault. Marvel did not hesitate to cut ties with him, firing Majors immediately after his conviction was announced. The actor was then sentenced in April 2024 to one year of domestic violence counseling. Related Stories Dua Lipa, Tame Impala and SZA to Headline Coachella 2027

With Majors’ firing, the Marvel Cinematic Universe would be overhauled, with “Avengers: The Kang Dynasty” being replaced by “Avengers: Doomsday.” The plan now moved to bringing back Robert Downey Jr. to the MCU, only this time not as Iron Man (who died in 2019’s “Avengers: Doomsday) but as the villainous Doctor Doom. However, Marvel Studios boss revealed in the latest issue of Empire magazine (via The Playlist) that Doom was in the conversation to be added to the MCU well before “The Kang Dynasty” fell apart amid Majors’ legal troubles.

“It probably would still have been called ‘The Kang Dynasty,’ but it would have been a set-up for Doom, midway through that movie,” Feige said, revealing the plan for “The Kang Dynasty” was actually for it to be a bait-and-switch movie in which Doom was revealed as the real Thanos-sized villain of the MCU’s multiverse saga.

According to Feige, Marvel first got in touch with Robert Downey Jr’s agent (telling him: “We have an idea, it’s time”) around the same time as the “Quantumania” premiere in February 2023, weeks before Majors’ arrest in New York City.

“It was very delicate,” Feige added about the Majors situation. “We didn’t want to rush into any rash decisions in terms of employment. People think there was a cause-and-effect with Jonathan’s issues, and that certainly accelerated some things. But the Doom of it all was well underway before that… ‘Quantumania’ was not received the way we would have liked. There are many elements of that that we’re proud of, the Kang performance being one of them. But we were changing [‘The Kang Dynasty’] even at that point.”

“Avengers: Doomsday” opens in theaters Dec. 18.

#725. CMA Awards Predictions: Expect Ella Langley to Get Everything but Male Vocalist, and Maybe Even That’s Not Safe

Variety is picking the winners for the 2026 CMAs, with plenty of easy-to-place bets on 9x-nominated Ella Langley. But it ain't over till the EOTY sings.

Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic

The suspense is unbearable: Will the 2026 CMA Awards see Ella Langley enjoying a total sweep, or just a near-sweep?

That is a real question, not a rhetorical one. But before we start trying to anticipate the math, let’s remember that, although Langley had a leading nine nominations, the most she can win is seven, because she is competing against herself in two categories, single of the year and song of the year, where “Choosin’ Texas” is up against “Be Her.” Normally that would leave room for vote-splitting, but rest assured, Langley and her two-stepping two-timers have the means to overcome that little problem. So with best single and best song utterly in the bag, that leaves five more open to see if she can run the board with the Country Music Association’s voters.

Entertainer of the Year, especially? There is some real suspense there. In some matters, it does take a crystal ball to see.

Here are our predictions for the winners of the 60th annual awards, which air live from Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena from 8-11 on the east coast and delayed for prime on the west coast, also at 8.

Luke CombsCody JohnsonElla LangleyChris StapletonLainey Wilson

Will win: Ella LangleyCould win: Cody Johnson

This top honor used to be regarded as something closer to an ongoing lifetime achievement award for a currently hot superstar than a recognition of pure, recent artistic achievement that could go to someone in the earlier stages of a long ascent. But it felt like that was starting to change when Lainey Wilson got it in 2023 without having developed any severe road wrinkles. (She also got it again in 2025.) All of which is to say that there is a question that could be asked with Lainey and this honor: “Too soon?” And the likely answer to that is: “Nope, but thanks for asking.”

Still, there is a lane open here for anyone to bust through if voters should decide that an armful of “lesser” awards are good enough for Langley this year. No one would greatly begrudge the well-love Wilson getting it for the third time in four years. Combs is probably the longest shot, being a two-time winner, like Langley. Neither Stapleton nor Johnson have gotten it even once. Stapleton has the “seriously, overdue” factor in his favor, having been nominated 11 times without ever taking it home. But if the enthusiasm for keeping it fresh continues but it’s just not Langley’s time for it, Johnson feels most like a presumptive second-place — and possibly first-place — finisher.

Still, the vast mainstream/crossover audiences watching the show at home will scratch their chins if it’s anyone but Langley, who has two of the biggest songs of the year in any genre in “Choosin’ Texas” and “Be Her” and has undoubtedly become country’s biggest ambassador to the world for this particular time frame. Choosin’ anyone else would just seem strangely insular.

“Be Her” – Ella Langley“Choosin’ Texas” – Ella Langley“I Knew It, I Knew You” – Taylor Swift“Somewhere Over Laredo” – Lainey Wilson“The Fall” – Cody Johnson

Will win: “Choosin’ Texas”Could win: Get real. Are you insane?

If “Choosin’ Texas” didn’t exist, we might be supposed that Langley would still be a front-runner for the award, but for “Be Her.” According to data provided to Variety by Luminate, “Be Her” is the all-around third most-consumed song of 2026 among all genres, not just country. But “Choosin’ Texas” is one of the biggest hits (use your Kanye voice here) of all time, as it currently enjoys a record-extending 28th week at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. Moreover, there is no resentment in the country community against its success, and certainly none against Langley for crossing over when the song America can’t stop falling for is as country as country can be. Seeing a shoo-in get shooed in never felt any better.

But, needless to say, boy, are the CMAs producers glad Taylor Swift is nominated here. Surely she knows she is not going to beat Langley here, and she is happy to show up and perform anyway… as a thank-you to the ones who brought her to the dance, and also, maybe, a campaign stop on the way to a place where more is at stake.

Ain’t In It For My Health – Zach TopDandelion – Ella LangleyMiddle of Nowhere – Kacey MusgravesParker McCollum – Parker McCollumThe Way I Am – Luke Combs

Will win: “Dandelion”Could win: “Parker McCollum”

It’s hard to imagine the scenario where an album as across-the-board as good as “Dandelion” doesn’t follow “Choosin’ Texas” into the winners’ circle. But there’s a case voters can reasonably make for casting their ballots for anything else in the category. Musgraves’ “Middle of Nowhere” was the most critically acclaimed country album of the year overall, and marked a definitive return to country after some musically farther-afield records from the star. It would be wonderful to see Kacey finally get it, many of us can agree. But only occasionally do voters go for an album that didn’t have a huge impact at mainstream country radio, as evidence by the fact that Musgraves’ often left-of-center approach has landed her four prior nominations in this category but only one win (for “Golden Hour”).

Still, this is the category where voters are most apt to sometimes break ranks with bestselling stuff and pick something cool to make a statement. (Think Lee Ann Womack’s “There’s More Where That Came From” in 2005.) So that could mean it’s back to being Musgraves’ time… or it could mean they’d have a hankering for Parker McCollum’s critically acclaimed, self-titled album, in which he was seen as going for artistry more than hits. The fact that the ACM Awards gave McCollum this award back in the spring definitely should be taken into account in reading the tea leaves. But realistically, it just seems like we’ll never know which of those albums came in second… because how can Langley lose?

SONG OF THE YEARAward goes to Songwriter(s)

“Be Her”Songwriters: Smith Ahnquist, Michael Hardy, Ella Langley, Jordan Schmidt“Beautiful Things”Songwriters: Jessi Alexander, Jessie Jo Dillon, Connie Harrington, Megan Moroney“Choosin’ Texas”Songwriters: Luke Dick, Ella Langley, Miranda Lambert, Joybeth Taylor“Dry Spell”Songwriters: Luke Laird, Shane McAnally, Kacey Musgraves, Josh Osborne“Gary”Songwriter: Stephen Wilson Jr.

Will win: “Choosin ’Texas”Could win: Get real, again.

It’s hard to remember when the CMA Awards had a greater crop of songs up for this honor than this year. Can they make it a five-way tie and everyone gets a prize? No, they cannot. So as much applause as we might want to hold in reserve for Musgraves, Megan Moroney or Stephen Wilson Jr., this particular prize has had Langley’s name on it since before the creation of the world. Not to get biblical.

Miranda LambertElla LangleyMegan MoroneyKacey MusgravesLainey Wilson

Will win: Ella LangleyCould win: No other option. The need to get real persists.

If you were making a list of the five most outstanding artists in country music in the 2020s, you could pick these five without any shame or need to move on… even if we might eventually worry we’d overlooked a guy or two. But honestly, what a field. Anyway it’s Langley’s to lose.

Luke CombsCody JohnsonChris StapletonZach TopStephen Wilson Jr.

Will win: Ella Langley. No, just kidding. Cody JohnsonCould win: Stephen Wilson Jr.

We should probably look at which three artists from this field are also nominated for entertainer of the year, and narrow it down from there. Of those three, Johnson has the freshest momentum, even though Combs and Stapleton are not a bit less popular than they ever were. You could never go wrong with virtually anyone in the world by naming Stapleton the male vocalist of this or any year, but he might have simply won it too many times. It would be a news-making upset if Wilson should get in — the odds are really stacked against him amid these proven heavyweights, but there is so much appreciation for him that a big cheer would go up if he crashed through that ceiling.

Lady ALittle Big TownMidlandOld DominionThe Red Clay Strays

Will win: The Red Clay StraysCould win: Old Dominion

The vocal group and vocal duo categories tend to have the least fresh blood and the most predictable year-by-year streaks The Red Clay Strays were a surprise winner last year — no one was more surprised than them — so it’ll be interesting to see if that was a one-off or the start of yet another CMA streak. I’m betting the latter, not least of all because they’re basically a rock group, and country people love having a real rock group — a good one — to bring some rootsy energy and fierceness into the genre.

Brooks & DunnBrothers OsborneDan + ShayMuscadine BloodlineThelma & James

Will win: Brooks & DunnCould win: Brothers Osborne

Just as much as CMA voters have liked having some new blood to vote for, in the form of the Red Clay Strays, they have enjoyed going back to Brooks & Dunn to celebrate old-home week. They’ve won this 16 times, and finally returned to the winners’ circle last year after previously last getting it in 2018. Their comeback as awardees here still feels fresh, in that sense, even if it’s a feat as old as time immemorial for them.

“A Song To Sing” – Miranda Lambert (with Chris Stapleton)“Horses and Divorces” – Kacey Musgraves (feat. Miranda Lambert)“I Can’t Love You Anymore” – Ella Langley & Morgan Wallen“If I Don’t Leave I’m Gonna Stay” – Carly Pearce & Riley Green“McArthur” – HARDY, Eric Church, Morgan Wallen & Tim McGraw

Will win: “I Can’t Love You Anymore”Could win: “Horses and Divorces”

This one is actually a tough category to call. The Langley/Wallen duet will probably get swept in on the wave that is pushing Ella toward so many other noms, and there continues to be support for Wallen in many pockets of the industry, even though you wouldn’t know it from the lack of nominations he’s gotten since winning entertainer of the year two years ago. But although their song served its purpose as something for them to sing together on his tour, is it really up there with Langley’s best songs or more of an agreeable time-passer? If it should fail to ride through on her long coattails, it’s tough to know where things go from there. I’m partial to the sensual Pearce/Green duet, and wish Pearce was up for a lot more for her excellent album.

But damn it, “Horses and Divorces” actually was an event, if you’re going to take the title of the trophy seriously. After a long, low-simmering feud no one denied, Musgraves had the brilliant idea to call Lambert up for a peace-pipe session, in the guise of a songwriting section about their feud… to great comedic-yet-real effect Talk about working it out on the remix. As Clint Eastwood once said, though, deserve’s got nothin’ to do with it. So expect Langley to need to build an extra shelf.

“Choosin’ Texas” – Ella Langley“Dry Spell” – Kacey Musgraves“Gary” – Stephen Wilson Jr.“The Fall” – Cody Johnson“White Horse” – Chris Stapleton

Will win: “Choosin’ Texas”Could win: “Dry Spell” or “Gary”

“Choosin’ Texas” isn’t really the most interesting video of all of these, but it gets the job done, and that should be enough to have it two-step its way into the winners’ circle. Still, maybe this is the place for voters to exercise a fondness for Musgraves, via her amusing video about sexual frustration in the supermarket. As Freud said, sometimes a cucumber is not just a cucumber.

Avery AnnaCarter FaithEmily Ann RobertsTucker WetmoreStephen Wilson Jr.

Will win: Tucker WetmoreCould win: Stephen Wilson Jr.

Wetmore is the only one here with No. 1 hits, which ought to be enough to push him across the line as voters face the inevitable question of how they think their choice will hold up 10 or 15 years from now. He’d be a worthy winner, but so would any of the others, most of all the critically beloved Faith and Wilson. Faith just picked up a key Grammy nomination… which of course means little in this context, but just saying… she’s interesting and she’s a keeper. So is Wilson, who has a much larger profile at present, including a lot of left-over love from how he killed it on last year’s telecast, twice. Wetmore is the horse to bet on, but this might be closer to a photo finish than most would suspect.

He served as head film buyer and oversaw Canadian operations and real estate ventures during his nearly three decades with the company.

Thom Velde, who served as head film buyer at AMC Theatres during his 27 years with the chain, died of cancer on Oct. 31 in Rancho Mirage, his family announced. He was 83.

Velde negotiated film agreements with domestic and international studios and oversaw AMC’s Canadian operations and real estate ventures during his long tenure at the company.

He was preceded in death by his wife, Kathy, and his daughter, Jennifer.

A celebration of life is set for 3 p.m. on Dec. 8 at Woodland Hills Community Church, with a reception to follow at the church.

Donations in his memory may be made to the Will Rogers Motion Picture Pioneers Foundation or to the Motion Picture & Television Fund, two organizations that serve the industry community and were “such an important part of his working life,” his family noted.

“Thom was an avid golfer and a devoted college football fan,” they continued. “Above all, he loved his family and friends, who will remember his strength of character, his generosity and the way he made time for the people in his life. He was always willing to lend a hand and had a special gift for keeping friendships alive over the years.”

#723. Scientists capture electrons making seemingly impossible quantum jumps

Physicists have captured an extraordinary quantum phenomenon in which electrons appear to leap across energy gaps that would normally be off limits. Using a new type of slow-motion electron camera, researchers were able to watch these incredibly fast movements in graphene, revealing how powerful electric fields can drive electrons between different energy states.

The effect is similar to stepping into an elevator and watching the floor display change from "1," "2," and "3" directly to "20." Instead of traveling through the seventeen floors in between, you somehow arrive at the twentieth floor. Although this sounds impossible in everyday life, electrons can make comparable jumps in the quantum world.

These unusual events are known as Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions. Physicists have long suspected that they could become increasingly important in high-speed semiconductor electronics, but observing exactly how they unfold has been a major challenge.

Now, researchers from the University of Regensburg, Philipps-Universität Marburg, and Forschungszentrum Jülich have directly tracked these transitions in graphene, a material made from an extremely thin layer of carbon atoms. Their findings, published in Nature, provide a detailed look at how electrons respond to intense electric fields generated by light.

How Electrons Cross Forbidden Energy Gaps

In semiconductors and similar materials, electrons are restricted to particular ranges of energy called energy bands. Between these bands are regions known as forbidden energy gaps, where electrons cannot ordinarily occupy stable states.

Under normal conditions, electrons tend to remain within their existing energy bands. However, the researchers observed something very different when they exposed graphene to intense pulses of light. The electric field accelerated the electrons and caused some of them to switch from one energy band to another, crossing the intervening gap through a quantum mechanical transition.

To capture these movements, the scientists developed an experimental technique that combines advanced laser technology with electron microscopy. This allowed them to examine electron behavior on timescales far too short for conventional imaging methods.

A Slow-Motion Camera Reveals Quantum Jumps

"If you want to know who has won a race, you have to watch all participants," explains Vincent Eggers, first author of the study. "Likewise, we must observe as many electrons as possible at one time to catch those that undergo a quantum mechanical transition while moving."

The key instrument is a photoemission momentum microscope. Rather than producing an enlarged picture of a material's surface, as a traditional microscope would, it measures the energies of electrons and how they are moving. Researchers then use this information to create detailed maps showing how electrons are distributed across different energy states.

One of the biggest technical obstacles was combining these measurements with powerful light fields that oscillate at extremely high speeds. The team needed to drive the electrons into motion while simultaneously recording how their energies and movements changed.

"Our team worked on this experiment for many years. Now, we can track electrons moving across the entire energy landscape of a solid in real time," says Rupert Huber.

Ulrich Höfer, a collaborator on the project and a pioneer in ultrafast electron spectroscopy, describes the excitement of witnessing the effect firsthand.

"Being able to observe such a fundamental quantum mechanical process during our first measurement campaign was a very special moment for us - it was also made possible by the samples we used."

Ultra-Pure Graphene Makes the Discovery Possible

The experiment depended on exceptionally pure graphene samples manufactured at Forschungszentrum Jülich. These specially prepared carbon layers were only one atom thick and had to be nearly flawless for the measurements to work.

"These precision experiments require material that is nearly perfect at the atomic level. This ensures that impurities do not obscure the delicate quantum dynamics of the electrons. Another important factor for the study was the use of "rotated" graphene, a specialty from Jülich, which allows the quantum dynamics to emerge particularly clearly," emphasizes Stefan Tautz from Forschungszentrum Jülich.

The carefully engineered material made it possible to distinguish the delicate quantum effects from interference caused by imperfections in the graphene.

What the researchers saw was remarkable. When exposed to sufficiently strong light fields, electrons crossed the forbidden energy gap with a transition probability reaching 100 percent.

This result highlights one of the most surprising features of Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions. Electrons can move between energy states with very high probability even when those states are separated by a substantial energy gap.

The crucial factor is how quickly the electrons approach the gap under the influence of the electric field. This makes the process fundamentally different from conventional quantum tunneling, in which particles pass through a barrier in physical space.

A New Path Toward Light-Controlled Electronics

Beyond revealing a fundamental quantum phenomenon, the new imaging technique could help scientists understand what prevents electrons from moving in a controlled and predictable way.

The graphene experiments have already provided an important clue. Although the electrons initially move in an orderly fashion, their interactions with the material's crystal lattice gradually disrupt that motion. Understanding these effects could help researchers develop more precise ways to control electron behavior.

This knowledge is particularly valuable for future electronic technologies that could use the extremely rapid oscillations of light to direct electrons instead of relying entirely on electrical voltages. Such approaches could open new possibilities for manipulating electronic properties at exceptionally high speeds.

The researchers also expect their method to work with many other quantum materials, allowing scientists to investigate previously inaccessible electron dynamics and potentially discover new ways to control them.

As Giacomo Inzani from the University of Regensburg explains, the achievement marks the beginning of a much broader exploration.

"Our experiment opens a panoramic window into the quantum world. Now, we can follow in real time how electrons move through the energy landscape of a material. And this is just the beginning. Our method can be applied to many other quantum materials, opening up completely new possibilities for controlling their electronic properties selectively with light."

#721. ‘Wicker’ Star Alexander Skarsgard Will Be Pushed Differently for Golden Globes Than Other Awards (Exclusive)

The Golden Globe winner's portrayal of a hunk made of twigs has left many audience members as smitten as — and even envious of — Olivia Colman's lonely fisherwoman who commissioned him.

Alexander Skarsgard, the Swedish actor who has garnered raves — and lust — for his portrayal of a hunk made of twigs in the eccentric dramedy Wicker, will be promoted in an unconventional way this awards season.

The Hollywood Reporter can exclusively report that the 50-year-old will be pushed by Wicker distributor Black Bear as a lead at the Golden Globes — specifically, in the category of best actor in a musical or comedy — but in the supporting category at the other major award shows where contests are not segregated by genre. Related Stories Business Alexander Skarsgard to Narrate Quinn Audio Erotica Original Set in World of 'Wicker' Movies 'Godzilla Minus Zero' Powers $31M in Historic Box Office Launch Against Subdued 'Cat in the Hat'

This path — lead for Globes, supporting for Oscars — has previously been employed by numerous others.

It worked well for some. Among them: Tatum O’Neal was nominated at the Globes and won at the Oscars for 1973’s Paper Moon; Maggie Smith won at both for 1978’s California Suite; Catherine Zeta-Jones was nominated at the Globes and won at the Oscars for 2002’s Chicago; and Alicia Vikander was nominated at the Globes and won at the Oscars for 2015’s The Danish Girl.

But it was less successful for others. For example, Cate Blanchett was nominated at the Globes but not at the Oscars for 2001’s Bandits; and Steve Carell was nominated at the Globes but not at the Oscars for 2017’s Battle of the Sexes.

A Black Bear rep tells THR, “We made the decision to position Alexander in lead actor for the Globes’ musical/comedy category because it gives the opportunity to recognize his unconventional romantic performance within the film’s unique blend of dark comedy, fantasy and romance. For other awards, where comedy and drama are not distinguished, supporting actor offers a more appropriate path to recognition reflecting the impact of his performance within the ensemble.”

Skarsgard, who won a Golden Globe for Big Little Lies in 2018 and was nominated for another for Succession in 2024, delivered his Wicker performance, opposite Oscar winner Olivia Colman, beneath elaborate WETA Workshop prosthetics and a full creature suit. Playing a character who barely speaks, the actor had to exaggerate his expressions in order for them to be visible, but not so much that they would seem over-the-top. The resulting nuanced, tender characterization, with much communicated through subtle gestures and soulful eyes, has left many audience members as smitten as — and even envious of — the lonely fisherwoman who commissioned the wicker man in the first place.

Wicker, based on the short story The Wicker Husband by Ursula Wills, was adapted for the screen and directed by Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson. Its strongest award prospects are probably in the best makeup and hairstyling and best visual effects Oscar races.

#720. A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding

Fossils provide an extraordinary window into Earth's distant past, revealing the animals, plants, and ecosystems that existed millions of years ago. Yet the fossil record tells only part of the story. Fossilization is exceptionally rare, meaning that just a tiny fraction of the organisms that once lived on Earth have been preserved. Even when fossils survive, scientists can only discover them if the rock layers containing them are accessible today.

As a result, our picture of prehistoric life is filled with major gaps. Some geological periods and parts of the world have produced abundant fossils, giving scientists a detailed understanding of the life that existed there. Other periods and regions remain largely unexplored. Because fossil excavations require considerable time and resources, knowing where to search could make a major difference in uncovering new evidence of ancient life.

To help solve this problem, Thomas A. Neubauer of the Bavarian State Collections of Natural History (SNSB) and Mathias Harzhauser of the Natural History Museum in Vienna have developed a new tool for guiding fossil research. The two paleontologists analyzed the geographic distribution of fossil discoveries from animals that inhabited shallow marine environments over the past 540 million years. For the first time, they also mapped the regions of the world where fossil information is missing, providing a clearer picture of where future discoveries may be possible.

Mapping 540 Million Years of Ancient Marine Life

To build their map, the researchers examined records from the Paleobiology Database (PBDB), the world's leading freely accessible repository of fossil information. The database contains a substantial portion of the paleontological findings published by scientists around the world.

Using these records, the team reconstructed where fossils from ancient shallow marine environments have been documented throughout Earth's history. They also examined how fossil research has developed over decades and centuries, measuring how frequently investigations in different regions have produced new scientific information.

The researchers then compared these findings with geological information from the Macrostat database. This allowed them to assess not only where fossils have already been discovered, but also where suitable rock formations could provide opportunities to fill important gaps in the fossil record.

Where Earth's Missing Fossils May Be Hiding

The analysis revealed a surprising imbalance in our understanding of prehistoric life. The Early Mesozoic (approx. 252 to 66 million years ago) and the Palaeozoic (approx. 539 to 252 million years ago) have already been studied extensively. According to the researchers, additional fossil discoveries from these periods are unlikely to produce a substantial increase in scientific knowledge in the near future.

The greatest opportunities for expanding the fossil record may instead lie in more recent geological history. Although scientists have already collected extensive evidence from the Cenozoic Era (beginning 66 million years ago), the analysis suggests that its shallow marine deposits still contain significant untapped potential for fossil discoveries.

To help researchers investigate this period, the team identified locations around the world where previously unknown fossil species are especially likely to be found. Crucially, these are also places where the appropriate geological layers are exposed or otherwise accessible, making actual discoveries possible.

A Treasure Map for Future Fossil Discoveries

By highlighting regions where important evidence may still be waiting, the new approach could help paleontologists plan more productive expeditions and make better use of limited research resources. Rather than concentrating on areas that have already been explored extensively, scientists can focus on locations with the greatest potential to reveal something new about Earth's prehistoric ecosystems.

"The fact that many regions of the Earth remain unexplored offers hope for valuable new discoveries," says SNSB paleobiologist Neubauer.

"But precisely because expanding the fossil record is quite challenging and progresses only slowly, our work can help researchers worldwide to focus their research specifically on these still largely unexplored areas. We provide a valuable guide for planning future projects and excavation campaigns. The same applies to the examination of existing museum collections awaiting scientific analysis. Through sensible prioritization, we can fill gaps in the fossil record strategically."

Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. The lives of NASA's Apollo astronauts depended on it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface.

Surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there. It took television pictures of the surface and learned about the composition of lunar soil. Then came the big liftoff.

First Surveyor 6 launched from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away. Next, Surveyor 6 took pictures of its original landing site. Flight controllers on Earth could see the landing pad prints of Surveyor 6. They also saw an imprint from the rocket exhaust when Surveyor 6 lifted off.

Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. Less than two years later, humans did the same thing during Apollo 11.

NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft launched to the moon on Nov. 7, 1967 and made its first landing on the lunar surface on Nov. 10 of that year. It's primary mission was to make a soft landing on the moon in the Sinus Medii of the moon.

The probe took nearly 30,000 photos of the moon during its 16 days on the lunar surface, with the lander shutting down due to the onset of lunar night on Nov. 26. Surveyor 6 was the sixth and penultimate moon mission of NASA's Surveyor lunar program, so a lot of what it did (launching and landing on the moon) had been done before.

But a lunar liftoff? That was something new.

"On November 17, as an engineering test to see if its rockets could be restarted on the Moon, Surveyor’s engines fired for 2.5 seconds, lifting the spacecraft 12 feet high and moving it 8 feet west of its original landing site, in the first powered liftoff from another celestial body," NASA wrote in a mission overview.

The engineering test proved that a spacecraft could land on the moon, and then lift off and take flight once more. That capability was a core requirement for NASA's Apollo astronaut moon landings that followed, since astronauts needed a way to return home after visiting the moon.

But there was critical science Surveyor 6 was able to do with the lunar hop.

"This maneuver provided excellent views of the surface disturbances produced by the initial landing and the effects of firing rocket engines close to the lunar surface," scientists with the Lunar and Planetary Institute wrote in a summary. "Photography obtained after the hop contributed to the soil mechanics investigation."

Surveyor 6 also had a bar magnet on its footpad that allowed scientists to test how magnetic the lunar regolith was at the landing site.

#718. Jeff Bezos Was ‘Heavily Involved’ in Casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond and Admits Initial Fears ‘Because He’s Already So Famous’

Amazon founder and chairman Jeff Bezos revealed during a recent appearance at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event that he was “heavily involved” in Amazon MGM casting Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.

Bezos said that because Bond is traditionally a star-making role, they were at first “slightly biased” against casting Pattinson because he’s already “so famous.” However, after narrowing down the candidates to five and conducting screen tests, he was the “obvious” choice. Related Stories Dua Lipa, Tame Impala and SZA to Headline Coachella 2027

“We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday,” Bezos said. “There was a big group initially, and we down-selected to five finalists. We did real, old-fashioned screen tests of those five finalists. It was interesting. Full costumes and real sets and other actors with them. We did three different scenes with each of the five finalists, and then we got together on Friday to spend a couple of hours looking at all the tests and reviewing all that.”

He continued, “By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance. It was immediately undebated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob. Initially, we were slightly biased against him just because he’s already so famous, like maybe we should have somebody more unknown, but in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”

Amazon MGM announced Pattinson as the next James Bond on Monday, ending weeks of rabid media speculation. “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” the “Batman” and “Primetime” star said in a statement after the news broke. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

While Bezos never mentioned them by name, industry analysts seemingly had a handle on the Bond finalists heading into the last weekend of casting. The shortlist of top choices included Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden and Nicholas Hoult. Other names rumored to be in the running at one include Jacob Elordi, Tom Francis, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Harris Dickinson and even Harry Styles.

Amazon finalized its deal for MGM, the studio behind James Bond, in 2022. However, it didn’t have creative control of the franchise until it bought out longtime Bond producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli for $20 million. Denis Villeneuve and Pattinson’s film will be the first released after the deal.

#716. Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent

Vaccines may do more than protect people from the immediate effects of a viral infection. New research suggests they could also help prevent lasting damage to the immune system that remains even after the virus has disappeared.

Scientists at Pompeu Fabra University discovered that mice recovering from an acute viral infection experienced prolonged problems with their immune defenses. Although the animals had successfully fought off the virus, their immune systems remained impaired, making it harder to respond to new threats. Remarkably, mice vaccinated before infection did not develop these problems, suggesting that vaccination may provide an additional layer of protection beyond preventing illness.

Most people think of common viral infections, such as colds or stomach viruses, as temporary illnesses. A virus enters the body, multiplies, causes symptoms, and is eventually brought under control by the immune system. Once symptoms disappear, recovery is generally considered complete. The immune response also creates protection against future encounters with the same virus.

But what if the immune system continues to experience harmful effects long after the infection appears to be over?

Viral Infections Can Leave Lasting Immune Damage

Researchers from Pompeu Fabra University's Infection Biology Laboratory investigated this possibility in a study published in Cell Death & Disease.

Using mice with acute viral infections, the team examined what happened to their immune systems after the animals had recovered. They found that eliminating the virus did not necessarily restore normal immune function. Instead, the infection left behind changes that persisted well beyond the initial illness.

According to Andreas Meyerhans, an ICREA research professor at UPF, who led the research, "there is a general perception that an acute viral infection is a relatively minor and transient event: once the virus is controlled and the symptoms have resolved, the body has fully recovered and is back to normal. But this view may underestimate consequences that are not immediately visible and can persist long after the infection itself has resolved."

The researchers traced these lingering effects to significant changes in the spleen, an organ that plays an important role in coordinating immune defenses. As the immune system fought to eliminate the virus, the spleen developed fibrosis, a condition involving the buildup of scar-like tissue. The arrangement and positioning of immune cells within the organ also became disrupted.

These structural changes interfered with the interactions between immune cells that are necessary to activate T cells. These specialized cells are essential to adaptive immunity because they help recognize and destroy infected cells.

As a result, the mice remained less capable of launching effective immune responses when exposed to new challenges. Even though the original infection had been brought under control, their immune defenses continued to function poorly.

"The infection can be controlled, but that does not necessarily mean that the host has fully recovered," says Dr. Paula Cebollada Rica, first author of the study. "Our findings show that the immune-related consequences of an acute viral infection can persist beyond the period in which the virus is detectable, leaving the animals in an immunocompromised state."

Vaccination Prevented Lasting Immune System Damage

After identifying these long-term effects, the scientists investigated whether they could be avoided. They focused on vaccination, which prepares the immune system to recognize and fight a pathogen before an infection occurs.

The results revealed a striking difference between vaccinated and unvaccinated animals. Mice that received vaccination before infection did not develop the spleen damage or immune dysfunction seen in the other group.

Their spleens maintained their normal structure, and their T cells continued to function at levels comparable to those of mice that had never been infected.

This finding suggests that vaccination can protect the immune system itself from some of the harmful consequences of fighting a viral infection. In the mouse model, vaccination not only protected against the disease caused by the virus but also preserved the animals' ability to respond to future immune challenges.

"Vaccinated animals did not experience T-cell dysfunction or splenic alterations after recovering from an acute viral infection. This means that vaccination not only prevented the disease resulting from the acute infection but also preserved the immune system's ability to cope with new challenges," Cebollada Rica explains.

A Hidden Benefit of Vaccines With Public Health Implications

The findings broaden the potential benefits of vaccination by highlighting a form of protection that may not be immediately apparent. Beyond reducing the immediate effects of an infection, vaccines may also help prevent persistent changes that weaken immune defenses.

Although these results were obtained in mice and do not establish that the same effects occur in humans, they raise important questions about how viral infections influence long-term immune health and how vaccination might help protect it.

The research also comes at a time when vaccination policies and infectious disease prevention efforts are increasingly influenced by political decisions. The researchers emphasize the importance of scientific evidence in understanding the full consequences of infections, particularly when policy choices can undermine coordinated efforts to prevent infectious diseases.

Understanding the broader benefits of vaccination could therefore influence not only medical care but also how public health officials explain the value of vaccines to the public.

"The benefits of vaccination highlighted by this research are important not only for healthcare, but also for how we communicate the value of vaccination to the population at large," Meyerhans states. "It is important that people are aware of the broader protection that vaccination can provide and continue to trust in vaccines as one of the most effective tools to prevent diseases. Put simply, vaccines provide strong health benefits at a relatively low cost to society."

#715. Netflix Eyes Return to Cannes After 10 Years as Festival Lobbies for Joel Coen’s ‘Jack of Spades,’ Starring Josh O’Connor

The streamer hasn't debuted a film at the festival since 2017.

The ice appears to be thawing between Netflix and Cannes.

The streamer, which hasn’t debuted a film at the festival in almost a decade due to France’s strict rules around theatrical releases, is eyeing a return to the south of France in 2027, Variety has learned. Ted Sarandos suggested as much earlier this year, when he told Variety he hoped to “do something special” for Cannes’ 80th edition. Related Stories Dua Lipa, Tame Impala and SZA to Headline Coachella 2027

Now it turns out that Cannes boss Thierry Frémaux has also been making a push to bring Joel Coen’s “Jack of Spades” to the festival for more than a year, sources say. Netflix declined to comment.

The American gothic mystery, starring Josh O’Connor, Patsy Ferran, Frances McDormand, Lesley Manville and Damian Lewis, was at one point expected to be ready for this year’s Cannes, then Venice, but is now on track for next May. Coen also has a strong relationship with Frémaux, who honored him alongside his brother Ethan at Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival.

But there’s a catch. Netflix recently acquired “Jack of Spades,” complicating plans for what would otherwise have been a natural Cannes contender.

That means the only way for Netflix to return to Cannes with “Jack of Spades” would be out of competition, which has been a deal-breaker for Sarandos. Sources say Frémaux has been trying to convince Netflix and Sarandos that an out-of-competition premiere can be just as prestigious as a competition slot, pointing to the recent examples of Martin Scorsese’s Apple-backed “Killers of the Flower Moon” and Tom Cruise’s “Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning,” both of which made a major splash on the Croisette without competing for the Palme d’Or.

But recent changes could help smooth the path towards a Netflix comeback on the Croisette. The streamer’s newly-appointed chief content officer Peter Rice is a longtime friend of Cannes who has known Frémaux since his days at Searchlight. His arrival could help bring the two sides closer after years of tensions over theatrical releases.

Netflix may also have good reason to seek a return to Cannes. After losing a few big-name filmmakers, the streamer could be looking to ramp up its prestige profile. While it has increasingly turned to Venice to launch major awards contenders, including Guillermo del Toro’s “Frankenstein” and Noah Baumbach’s “Jay Kelly,” Cannes remains the world’s biggest film festival and arguably the most powerful platform for launching auteur-driven movies.

Netflix knows that better than most. Despite not bringing its own movies to the festival in 10 years, it has snapped up several on the ground there. In 2024, it bought Jacques Audiard’s “Emilia Pérez” which went on earn 13 Oscar nominations and win two Oscars, including best actress for Zoe Saldana. This year, it acquired “La Bola Negra,” now its main hope for awards season — with many tipping it for best picture.

“Jack of Spades” would seem a perfect fit for the festival, where Joel Coen is one of its favorite auteurs. Alongside his brother Ethan, the director has brought films including “Barton Fink,” which won the Palme d’Or and best director awards, “No Country for Old Men” and “Inside Llewyn Davis.”

Netflix hasn’t taken a film to Cannes since 2017, when it premiered both Bong Joon-ho’s “Okja” and Noah Baumbach’s “The Meyerowitz Stories.” It sparked an outcry from French exhibitors, prompting the festival to change its rules the following year to require competition films to receive theatrical releases in France.

The streamer has, however, softened its stance on theatrical releases considerably. “La Bola Negra” is in the middle of a 46-day theatrical rollout, the longest Netflix has given any of its films to date. Next year, “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” will have an exclusive theatrical run, as will Taika Waititi’s animated take on Roald Dahl, “Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory.”

#714. Thom Velde, Former AMC Theatres Executive, Dies at 83

Thomas Velde, who served as head film buyer at AMC Theatres during his 27 years at the exhibitor, died Oct. 31. He was 83.

Velde died of cancer at his home in Rancho Mirage, Calif..

For 27 years, he worked at AMC Theatres, where he negotiated film agreements with domestic and international studios while also overseeing the entertainment company’s Canadian operations and real estate ventures. Following his time at AMC, he worked independently in motion picture distribution and would consult for clients that included Microspace Communications and CJ America. Velde is survived by his wife, Deborah; his daughters, Andrea Ter-Velde and Courtney Ter-Velde, and their husbands, John McLoughlin and Greg Horton; his son, Sam; stepsons Matthew Castillo and Spencer Castillo and their wives, Crissy Castillo and Claire Castillo; grandchildren Aubrey Long and Jack Long; and step-grandchildren Jackson Castillo, Sammy Castillo, Cruz Castillo, Bianca Castillo and Capri Castillo.

A celebration of life will be held Dec. 8 at 3 p.m. at Woodland Hills Community Church. Donations can be made to the Will Rogers Motion Picture Pioneers Foundation or the Motion Picture and Television Fund, both of which serve the industry community Velde was a part of.

“Thom was an avid golfer and a devoted college football fan,” his family noted. “Above all, he loved his family and friends, who will remember his strength of character, his generosity and the way he made time for the people in his life. He was always willing to lend a hand and had a special gift for keeping friendships alive over the years.”

#712. 5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings

New forensic evidence suggests that some of ancient Egypt's earliest rulers had members of their royal households killed when they died, possibly so those individuals could continue serving them in the afterlife. The discovery sheds new light on a disturbing burial practice that archaeologists suspected more than a century ago but could not prove.

The evidence comes from ancient skulls recovered near royal tombs at Abydos, Egypt, where members of the First Dynasty were buried roughly 5,000 years ago. When archaeologist Flinders Petrie excavated the graves in the 1920s, he noticed that unusually large numbers of people had been buried around the kings. He suspected that these individuals had been sacrificed following their rulers' deaths, but he could not identify physical evidence of fatal injuries.

Now, a modern forensic examination has uncovered signs of potentially deadly head trauma in 18 of 46 skulls, representing approximately 39% of the individuals studied. The findings provide compelling new support for the theory that human sacrifice played a role in the burial traditions of ancient Egypt's first kings.

"I was drawn to these retainers partly because, even though they were buried around royalty, they are mostly relegated to footnotes in the grander narrative," said Dr. Roselyn Campbell of Purdue University, who led the research published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. Campbell is also the author of the forthcoming book State-sanctioned Violence and Human Sacrifice in Early Dynastic Egypt (Routledge Press).

"Who were these people and how did they view the ruler and their own role in his or her life and death?"

A 5,000-Year-Old Mystery Surrounding Egypt's First Kings

Around 3000 BCE, the earliest kings of a unified Egypt constructed elaborate burial complexes at Abydos. These sites included royal tombs, additional burial chambers, and enclosed areas believed to have been used for funeral ceremonies.

Surrounding the main structures were numerous smaller graves arranged in rows. Some royal burial sites were accompanied by hundreds of these subsidiary burials, raising questions about why so many people had been buried in close association with a single ruler.

"Each subsidiary burial was a simple chamber in a row of dozens of others," said Campbell. "Some people had a simple coffin. Most people had a few grave goods, like ceramic vessels, and many graves also included small objects like copper tools, projectile points, or small ivory figurines. Petrie found a few grave markers that had names and sometimes official titles on them. The titles seem to mostly refer to lower- or mid-level officials as well as artisans."

The extraordinary concentration of graves led Petrie to propose that the people buried alongside the kings were victims of a practice known as retainer sacrifice.

"Retainer sacrifice is a type of human sacrifice where those close to a ruler are killed when the ruler dies," explained Campbell. "In many cultures, retainer sacrifice is practiced because of beliefs that the sacrificed individuals will continue to serve the ruler in some kind of afterlife, but retainer sacrifice can also be a visceral display of the ruler's power. Some retainers might have volunteered to die to achieve eternal life or honor, others may have been chosen or even forced."

Despite the suspicious circumstances, Petrie could not find convincing evidence that the individuals had died violently. Without identifiable fatal injuries, the possibility of human sacrifice remained an unresolved archaeological mystery.

Campbell decided to revisit the original excavation evidence, hoping that modern forensic techniques could reveal clues that had escaped investigators a century earlier.

Modern Forensics Reveals Evidence of Violent Deaths

Although Petrie documented his excavations carefully, he eventually reburied most of the human remains. He did, however, preserve a selection of skulls, some of which were transferred to the United Kingdom.

Campbell located 46 of these skulls in the Duckworth Collection at Cambridge University and examined them using contemporary forensic knowledge.

The results revealed injuries that had previously gone unrecognized. Eighteen skulls showed substantial cranial trauma, primarily in the form of linear fractures. Petrie had apparently interpreted these cracks as damage caused by natural processes rather than injuries sustained by living people.

Modern forensic methods made it possible to identify the fractures as perimortem injuries, meaning they occurred around the time of death. Their characteristics suggest that some of the individuals may have suffered deliberate, potentially fatal blows to the head.

"The injuries on the preserved crania are generally linear fractures, which would likely cause rapid unconsciousness, internal bleeding, and death," said Campbell, who also reported evidence of sharp-force trauma on some of the 18 skulls, including a chopping injury to one individual's eye.

These findings suggest that at least 39% of the examined individuals may have been deliberately killed, providing important new evidence in support of the long-standing human sacrifice hypothesis.

How Were Ancient Egypt's Royal Attendants Killed?

Although the skull injuries offer strong evidence of violence, the precise circumstances of the deaths remain uncertain.

Ancient Egyptian artwork frequently portrays kings striking enemies with maces, but Campbell noted that the royal attendants buried at Abydos were not enemy combatants. The injuries also do not match the damage typically associated with these weapons.

A mace would generally produce depressed skull fractures, while the injuries identified in this study were predominantly linear. Such fractures are more commonly associated with impacts from broad, flat objects or severe falls.

Accidental falls cannot be entirely excluded. However, a fall powerful enough to fracture the skull would likely have caused injuries elsewhere in the skeleton. Such damage should have appeared in Petrie's excavation records or photographs, yet no corresponding evidence was documented.

The researchers also cannot determine how the remaining individuals died. Some may have died naturally, while others could have been killed using methods that left no recognizable marks on their bones, such as asphyxiation.

Additional injuries might also have been found if the rest of their skeletons were available for examination. Unfortunately, most of those remains were reburied more than a century ago, leaving researchers with only part of the physical evidence.

Ancient Skulls Reveal New Clues to Egypt's Dark Past

The findings demonstrate how archaeological collections can preserve important clues long after their original excavation. Even when evidence is incomplete, advances in scientific techniques can provide new answers to questions that earlier researchers were unable to resolve.

For Campbell, the possibility of locating and examining the remaining skeletal material offers an especially intriguing opportunity to learn more about the people buried around Egypt's earliest kings.

"If I had unlimited resources, I would love to figure out where the bodies of these individuals might be and analyze them!" said Campbell. "Still, this study shows how much new information about the past can be revealed when we revisit previous data armed with updated methods and knowledge, even for datasets that are incomplete and imperfect like this one."

"Early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance."

The failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17).

That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement.

"While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's update.

The two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five launches under its belt.

The new rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff.

On both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security launches with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle issue. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.)

That work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA said in an Oct. 28 update. And those tweaks apparently worked.

"All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the company wrote in today's update.

Vulcan's Centaur V upper stage, which features two RL-10C engines, did its job as well "but was unable to recover from the [booster] performance loss, resulting in loss of mission," ULA added.

Vulcan's first-stage booster is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are built by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. Today's update did not identify the exact problem with the booster; doing so will require more time, as the investigation has just begun.

If that investigation finds a serious issue with the BE-4, there could be broad ripple effects across the American space program. After all, that engine also powers the first stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which is a key piece of hardware for NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. (And New Glenn is currently recovering from a failure of its own — a massive explosion on the test stand that occurred on May 28.)

NASA plans to integrate the Centaur V upper stage into its Space Launch System moon rocket, the vehicle that launches Artemis astronauts to space. So the fact that the Centaur performed nominally on Sunday is a bit of good news for the space agency.

Vulcan's grounding is a big deal, no matter what the anomaly investigation ends up finding. The U.S. doesn't have a surfeit of powerful rockets, after all, and two of them — Vulcan and New Glenn — are out of commission at the moment.

There's considerable pressure on both Vulcan and New Glenn to bounce back strong, for the nation faces an impending launch crunch in the next few years. SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets and shift its launch load over to the fully reusable Starship megarocket. SpaceX is expected to prioritize its own needs in Starship's early days, using the vehicle primarily to build out its next-gen Starlink broadband constellation and Starmind AI data center network.

The Vulcan failure also impacts Amazon — specifically, the company's plan to build out Amazon Leo, which will compete with SpaceX's Starlink. Amazon has booked about 100 launches on a variety of rockets to build its constellation, which will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Thirty-eight of those bookings are for Vulcan; Sunday's launch was the first of those.

The other rockets Amazon has booked are the Atlas V, New Glenn, Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. About 400 operational Amazon Leo satellites have reached orbit to date across 14 launches (not including Sunday's failure).
