It comes down to choices made for speed and science, as the two spacecraft flew by planets in the 1970s and 1980s.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference?

On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky.

But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA.

The original aim of both the spacecraft, which launched about two weeks apart in 1977 with Voyager 2 going first, was to look at Jupiter and Saturn. If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of Titan, before flying outside the plane of the solar system.

NASA had a range of trajectory options to consider when launching the spacecraft, and elected to bring Voyager 1 at a faster trajectory — as illustrated in this video by Britannica, where you can quickly see the spacecraft overtaking Voyager 2 on its way to Jupiter even though Voyager 1. Voyager 1 arrived at Jupiter on March 5, 1979 while Voyager 2 got there four months later on July 9.

Each of the spacecraft then performed a "gravity assist"—a sort of slingshot around the planet in which they took a tiny bit of momentum from Jupiter to gain speed as the spacecraft flew to Saturn. This technique is used constantly, such as recently when the ESCAPADE Mars mission flew two spacecraft by Earth on the way to the Red Planet, as it allows spacecraft to gain speed while saving on fuel. The planets themselves don't slow down that much.

"Because the planet is so much more massive than the spacecraft, the transfer doesn't affect the planet to any measurable extent, but to the spacecraft it's a big deal," the Planetary Society wrote. "For example, we can calculate that during the Voyager encounters with Jupiter in 1979, Jupiter slowed down by roughly 10 to the -24th power kilometers per second — a change much too small to measure."

"But each Voyager gained about 10 km/s [6.2 miles/s], a pretty big number," the society continued about the Jupiter encounter. This was "enough to put them on a fast path to Saturn — and in the case of Voyager 2, to Uranus and Neptune as well — and eventual escape from the solar system."

With each flyby, the two spacecraft picked up speed with a single exception — during Voyager 2's encounter of Neptune. That's because the spacecraft made a turn to fly by Triton. The maneuver brought Voyager 2 over Neptune's north pole, before it turned and then was directed to begin "plunging down, out of the plane of the solar system," losing speed along the way.

Voyager 2, in fact, did not have enough speed to leave the solar system until it flew by Jupiter. "It gained about 10 km/s at Jupiter, about 5 km/s at Saturn, about 2 km/s at Uranus, and lost about 2 km/s at Neptune," the Planetary Society wrote of the speeds, which are 6.21 miles/s, 3.11 miles/s, 1.24 miles/s and a loss of 1.24 miles/s, respectively.

At any rate, these fast speeds allowed both spacecraft not only to go fast, but to eventually reach interstellar space in 2012 (Voyager 1) and 2018 (Voyager 2), respectively. With the light-day milestone now reached by Voyager 1, it is anticipated the spacecraft could work into the 2030s, as long as their nuclear power sources can last.

NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which manages the mission, has been carefully turning off instruments as required, and recently did a "Big Bang" procedure on both spacecraft to redistribute power supplies as best as possible. The idea is to maximize science return on both spacecraft, the only interstellar messengers we have, for as long as possible.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#688. Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns

The European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 exceptionally ancient quasars, including two that have set new records as the earliest ever observed. These brilliant galactic centers, powered by enormous black holes, were already radiating as much light as a trillion Suns when the Universe was only 670 million years old, about 5% of its present age.

Quasars are among the brightest objects in the cosmos. They appear during a relatively short period in a galaxy's history when huge quantities of gas and other material spiral toward its central supermassive black hole. This process releases extraordinary amounts of energy, causing the galaxy's core to shine hundreds or even thousands of times more brightly than the rest of the galaxy combined.

Astronomers have spent decades searching for quasars from the Universe's earliest years because they offer valuable clues about the formation of the first galaxies and supermassive black holes. Finding them, however, is extremely challenging. Few galaxies had grown large enough to host such objects at that early stage, and the light reaching us today is incredibly faint. These distant sources can also be difficult to distinguish from stars much closer to Earth.

Launched in 2023, Euclid is transforming that search. Its ability to survey enormous regions of the sky and detect faint objects has already produced an unprecedented collection of 31 quasars from the early Universe, including some dating back to when the cosmos was just 5% of its current age.

"These early quasars date back to the Universe's infancy," says Daming Yang of Leiden University in the Netherlands, lead author of the Euclid discovery paper. "By finding and studying them, we can better understand how these enormous systems formed and grew so quickly - one of the greatest mysteries in astrophysics."

Euclid Reveals a Hidden Population of Ancient Quasars

Until now, astronomers had identified only a small fraction of the quasars that existed during the Universe's earliest period. Most known examples were exceptionally luminous objects that stood out because they were easier to detect. This limited sample made it difficult to understand the broader population and how these powerful systems developed.

Euclid is changing that picture by identifying not only the brightest quasars but also much fainter examples that previous searches struggled to find. Its discoveries are providing scientists with a far more representative view of the ancient quasar population, opening the door to more detailed studies of these early cosmic objects.

"Euclid is a true game-changer," adds Daming. "Before, we could only find a handful of the very brightest ancient quasars, but Euclid lets us search far more efficiently across huge areas of sky to capture much fainter light. It's a unique tool for quasar hunting."

Among the 31 newly identified quasars, 12 have a redshift of 7 or greater. Redshift describes how light is stretched as the Universe expands and helps astronomers determine how far away an object is and how far back in cosmic history its light originated. A redshift of at least 7 places these quasars within the Universe's first 770 million years.

Two Record-Breaking Quasars From Cosmic Dawn

Two objects stand out as particularly extraordinary. The most ancient, EUCL J172902.75+641018.1, has a redshift of 7.77, while EUCL J125308.55+705432.3 has a redshift of 7.69. Both are located just over 13 billion light-years from Earth and were already shining within the first 670 million years of cosmic history.

These discoveries establish new records for the earliest known quasars. The previous record belonged to an object discovered in 2021, which has a redshift of 7.64.

"This finding more than doubles the number of quasars we know of that are so ancient," says Antonio La Marca, an ESA Research Fellow in the Euclid team.

The pace of discovery is especially remarkable. Astronomers needed more than a decade to identify roughly the first 10 quasars with redshifts of 7 or higher. Euclid has already surpassed that number in just one year, demonstrating how dramatically the telescope is accelerating research into the early Universe.

"The Euclid team has taken a true 'census' of quasars at the dawn of the Universe for the first time," adds Antonio. "It's a big step towards understanding these fascinating objects on a more fundamental level."

Ancient Black Holes Reveal Clues About the First Galaxies

One of the newly discovered objects is already offering additional insight into conditions during the Universe's infancy. Silvia Belladitta and colleagues recently conducted a more detailed investigation of the second most ancient quasar identified by Daming and his team.

Their observations revealed that the quasar sits inside a galaxy filled with gas and dust where new stars are forming at a tremendous rate. This provides an important glimpse of the environment surrounding an early supermassive black hole and could help researchers understand how the first massive galaxies evolved alongside the black holes at their centers.

These quasars also belong to a transformative chapter in cosmic history known as the epoch of reionization. During this period, the Universe emerged from a cold, dark state (the 'dark ages') as increasingly energetic radiation heated the surrounding gas and ionized it (split apart by energetic light). This fundamental transition helped establish the conditions that shaped the Universe we observe today.

"Ancient quasars are rare discoveries. They're interesting in themselves, but also time machines that enable us to explore the early Universe and understand how the first generation of galaxies came to be," says ESA Euclid Project Scientist Valeria Pettorino.

How Euclid Is Transforming the Search for Cosmic Giants

Euclid's success comes from a powerful combination of capabilities. The telescope can examine enormous portions of the sky while collecting detailed images and detecting faint infrared light from extremely distant objects. Together, these features make it exceptionally effective at finding rare sources that earlier surveys could easily miss.

"Euclid's capabilities are unrivaled. The telescope combines a large area, depth, sharp imaging, and unique space-based infrared vision in a way that lets us pick out rare, extremely distant objects far more efficiently than before.

"And it's not just the telescope: the data processing is only possible thanks to thousands of Euclid Consortium scientists and engineers working together to deliver scientific discoveries, sifting through enormous datasets to identify rare, distant quasars that we can study further using telescopes on the ground."

All 31 quasars were identified using observations from the Euclid Wide Survey, an ambitious project that will eventually examine more than one-third of the entire sky.

Although Euclid's primary mission is to investigate the dark Universe, its observations are revealing much more. By studying billions of galaxies, the telescope is helping astronomers investigate the Universe's composition, history, evolution, and vast cosmic structure. At the same time, its sweeping survey is uncovering rare ancient quasars that offer a remarkable opportunity to explore how the first galaxies and giant black holes emerged.

As Euclid continues mapping the cosmos, astronomers expect its growing collection of distant quasars to provide new clues about one of astrophysics' most enduring questions: how supermassive black holes became so enormous in such a remarkably short time after the Big Bang.

#687. The 4 Best Planners of 2027: Roterunner, Hobonichi, Cloth & Paper

There’s nothing like the feeling of a brand-new planner, and I've found the best planners if you're shopping for something new for 2027. Whether you're looking to get a little more organized or just love having somewhere to write everything down, the beginning of the year is a great time for a fresh start, and most planner companies have their 2027 planner designs already available.

The world of planners might seem simple if you've only browsed your local Target or bookstore to see what planners they might have on hand. But there's a wide world of options out there that can perfectly suit your needs, especially if you're willing to build your own travel notebook or write in the dates on an undated paper planner, or open to trying your first Japanese-style planner.

After years of testing and a constant stack of planners on my desk, I've found these standout favorite planner styles that could benefit everyone. If you're looking for a tech companion to your paper planner, check out my guides to the Best Digital Wall Calendars and Best Digital Notebooks to help keep your calendar and thoughts organized digitally.

Updated November 2026: I've updated the information in this guide to reflect planner availability as 2026 comes to an end and 2027 designs become available. I'm also currently testing 2027 designs from Plum Paper, Laurel Denise, My PA Planner, and Sterling Ink, plus an undated design of Aura Estelle if you're looking for a planner you can start using in December 2026 into the new year.

If you need a single planner that can do it all and won't burn through your back-to-school budget, this is the one. The Roterunner Purpose Planner is an undated planner that has monthly spreads, weekly spreads, and two full open pages for each week, so there's plenty of room to write longer lists or a project brainstorm. Each monthly and weekly spread has a ton of premade checklist sections for you to use, too. There's even space to track your meals, water intake, and gratitude. It's a planner that actually helps me stay organized and gives me space to track and take notes without running out of room.

The undated nature makes it easy to pick up anytime and use for whichever months you need. Fell off the boat for a few months? No problem. No pages will go to waste when you can fill them in as you go. It only covers six months, but I actually like that; it once again feels like a feasible commitment, especially if you're waffling on how much paper planner you want to promise to use. I love the massive B5 size ($35) since it's finally enough space for me and all my various to-do lists and brainstorms, but there's also a smaller (and cheaper!) A5 ($28) size. It's truly my go-to planner since it has so much space for me to both use the pre-made lists and the open space to actually stay organized and put all my ideas, plans, and notes into one planner. Most others make me feel like I need a companion notebook, but not the Roterunner.

The covers come in a variety of simple colors, and in both hard cover or soft, but the butter-soft faux leather soft cover is my favorite of the bunch. Get it in B5 size if you're always looking for more room in your journals and planners—you won't regret it.

If you're getting into planners, there's no way you won't hear about Hobonichi at some point. There are a few different planners the brand makes, with the Techo being the most popular model. I tested the similar Hobonichi Cousin, which adds weekly spreads to the front of the planner after the monthly overviews. While I don't typically prefer a daily planner style, I was surprised by how much I liked using the Hobonichi. All of Hobonichi's planners use Tomoe River S paper, which is super thin but won't bleed through to the other side. It's also super smooth to the touch and to write on. I liked adding my own structure to the daily pages; I sketched a box to separate my to-do lists and habit trackers from my hourly agenda for the day, and then would usually freeform the rest of the page based on what was on my mind. The Cousin I tested and photographed is an A5 size, while the standard Techo is the smaller A6.

Hobonichi's 2027 editions are here, so you can stock up on your planner for next year right now, plus tons of colors, covers, and other accessories, some of which are unique to 2027. I recommend picking out a protective cover since I did ding up my soft cover quite a bit, and that was just from being used around the house with an occasional trip in a bag. There are little quotes in the corners, but I got a Japanese version instead of an English one, so I can't actually read mine. But honestly, I'm glad I did; I prefer the Japanese lettering to English words on the corners of each page.

I've been obsessed with travel notebooks this year. A travel notebook uses bands to connect three or four notebooks together, and I love using this system to build a customized planner designed for my exact needs. It makes it easy to change the design, too, since you can just switch out a single notebook when it's full.

I really like Cloth & Paper's Travel Notebook Collection. There are 13 different notebooks you can choose from to include in your travel notebook, ranging from classic weekly and monthly spreads to more unique options like a daily wellness notebook and a task planner. It's really a great option if you want a couple of specific things, or even just a regular monthly and weekly notebook plus a blank notebook in the back you can fill with to-do lists and replace anytime without needing an entirely new planner. It's great for students, too, because you can have a notebook dedicated to tracking your assignments and syllabus for the semester. You'll need to create your own, though, as Cloth & Paper doesn't have a dedicated academic notebook for you to select.

I tried both the A5 Slim and the Pocket Plus size, and I really prefer the A5 Slim for a traditional planner experience. The Pocket Plus would be fun to bring on a trip; I wish I'd had it on my latest trip to store little mementos and important things like parking receipts, and could have also written out notes and the plan for the week-long trip. But otherwise, the larger A5 slim was much easier to write on and use for my daily notes and planning.

You'll want the Clear Vinyl Travel Notebook Cover ($23 to $25) no matter which size you choose, which includes elastic bindings to bring all the notebooks you buy together, and you can also pick up more colorful elastic options to add a little more personality to your planner.

I've heard a lot of good things about Erin Condren. Founded in 2005 by Erin Condren, it's known for the LifePlanner that's full of various spreads and productivity tools that you can customize, but there are other variations of planners you can find from the brand. While you'll usually customize your Erin Condren planner if you shop directly on the site, there's a predesigned Target line you can shop that won't give you options, but will give you a well-made planner that's ready to go immediately.

I've been testing the Erin Condren Academic Planner you'll find at Target, but it's sold out as we head into the new year; Erin Condren's website has similar, but more expensive options with more cover and customization options. This base version from Target is a great fit for students and people with deadline-style or client-based work they want to organize. Each month has two pages following the monthly spread to set your most important to-dos and dates, but also a full page to track the month's deadlines and what class (or client, or in my case, story beat) they're for. After that, there are weekly spreads with long columns for each day, and seven blocks of four lines that you can label with things like specific classes, clubs, or organizations, or parenting and household tasks, as I track. It's been a really easy planner to add into my lifestyle, even though it's made for students. There's a class tracker in the front of the planner, too, which I skipped using, plus a detailed holiday calendar, and the back has project and exam pages, plus blank note pages, and even a simple sheet of stickers with things like “Exam,” “Midterm,” and “Paper Due.”

Academic planners usually start in August, so you probably don't want a planner like this if you want something fresh for the new year. But it's still my favorite I've tried if it's your preferred style. Erin Condren does have annual layouts and its popular LifePlanner designs available in 2027 layouts, and other specific designs like budget planners and teacher lesson planners if you're looking for something specific, too.

Like I said, there's a huge world of planners out there. Here are a few that the Reviews team and I at WIRED have tested and enjoyed.

The Kokuyo Jibun Techo is another Japanese planner, but this one is a travel-notebook-style design, making it more customizable with a cover and multiple books that fit inside it. The First Kit comes with three books that fit into the included cover: Diary (labeled simply with the year), Life, and Idea. The 2026 versions are sold out, but you can buy the 2027 versions right now.

Looking for more of a monthly planner? The Big A## Planner is a massive planner with a nice monthly spread you can literally spread across your desk, with plenty of writing space for each day. Best for working from home, though; you don't want to have to fit this into your work bag.

If you're looking for a great daily planner, the Day Designer is a popular option for a reason. It's bulky since it has pages for every single day, but it leaves room for both your schedule and a long to-do list.

Plum Paper is my favorite classic-style planner, and you can easily customize it to start at any time of year and design the pages to fit your needs. I especially like the weekly A5 Vertical Priorities layout, and you can add all kinds of customizations into the daily columns, the habit tracker, and more to make it exactly what you want. But I've also left the habit tracker blank so I can adjust my habits as needed all year long.

I bought this no-frills hardback during Prime Day last year, figuring I couldn’t go wrong for less than 20 bucks, and I was right. It’s a handy A5 size with a monthly view calendar at the beginning of each month, and then a 5-by-2.5-inch square for each day. That’s it. There are some plain lined pages in the back if you need more space for notes, but if your planning consists only of to-do lists and tracking deadlines, you will love this.—Kat Merck

Agendio Basic Planner starting at $48: This is a completely customizable planner. I liked it, and you have the option to design your own pages, and the folder-style cover will protect both the pages and binding. I didn't love the customization tools or abilities as much as I wanted to, and there are a lot of steps to create your planner. I preferred the custom tools of Plum Paper over it. It's a good planner if the pages and binder-style are what you're looking for, and you can find some preset options that usually start around $48 for the smallest page size and black-and-white print.

Ban.do 12-Month Planner for $20: If you're looking for another affordable option but want something with more personality than the Roterunner above, Ban.do's planners are fun and colorful and even come with a page of stickers. It's only a horizontal weekly format, though, which I don't love (but maybe you do!) and the 2027 12-Month designs are now available.

Happy Planner 12-Month Planner for $33: Happy Planner uses disc-bound planners to make it easy to remove and add pages or covers, which is nice for customizability. But they're a very specific aesthetic, and personally, I didn't love turning pages on the discs. Still, it's a good planner if you like the style, and they come in a ton of different layouts. Right now, you can get a Happy Planner that starts in July 2026 and will run you until June 2027, perfect for tracking the academic year.

Laurel Denise Nancy Academic Planner for $44: These planners are cool because you'll look at the month and your weekly at the same time, as the slim weekly pages lay on top of the monthly spread. However, I write way, way too much for the space in these planners, at least for the Nancy design I tested previously. It's great if you just want to write a couple to-dos and meetings per day, but if you want space for detailed lists, you might feel the way I did. I'm currently testing the 2027 Luna ($62) and Scout ($62) planners from Laurel Denise to see if I still feel the same way compared to the original design.

Leuchtturm1917 12-Month Ruled Planner for $29: This is a solid, minimalist planner that has a popular following. It's a simple horizontal weekly layout with the week on one side and a lined page on the other. It's not enough space for everything I write down, but if you're looking for something simple and space for a couple of lists or notes for each week that fit onto a page, it's a good option for you. Leuchtturm1917 also has a nice line of notebooks that look the same from the outside cover, so make sure you actually get the planner.

Muji Undated Weekly Planner for $7: If you want a super simple, super affordable planner, the Muji Undated Weekly is for you. It's just undated weekly horizontal spreads from front to back, even on the paper cover. It's slim, but still more than a year's worth of weeks in it. It's the most minimalist planner I've tried, and though I'm not a fan of horizontal weekly spreads for my planner needs, it's a great cheap option for a lot of people.

Papier Hardcover 2027 Planner for $40: My favorite thing about Papier's planners is how gorgeous the covers are. Papier has a range of beautiful designs you can choose that feel like they belong on a bookshelf rather than just my planner. I tested one of the annual planners, which has the horizontal weekly layout I don't love on any planner (and you can still get that by choosing the mid-year layout for any cover Papier has if you love that style), but the academic one ($29) has a vertical layout that's much more up my alley. Whichever style you like, you can pick. Papier also has softcover academic planners ($32) that use a ring binding, which is easier to lay open than the hard cover binding, and still has both mid-year and academic layout options.

Passion Planner 2027 Planner for $50: This planner was really popular when I was in college, and maybe it still is with the college kids. I liked it, but I feel like the Purpose Planner does a similar thing but better, at least for my needs. It's got vertical spread, but every slot is timed, so I can't use it as a to-do list. It's great for anyone needing to plan out a super detailed schedule and has some to-do list spaces on the bottom, but they're pretty small in my opinion to work for an entire week. It's good for students who only want to track their busy schedules and a couple assignments and tasks for each week.

Looking for what to pair with your planner? Here are some of our team's favorite daily tools and planner accessories.

Passion Planner Passion Highlighters for $20: If your planner could use a little color, I really like Passion Planner's highlighter sets. They're nice and thin-tipped to fit into slim planner lines, and I especially like the vintage colors for adding color without it feeling neon-bright. You can use the highlighters to organize your plans by type (I like to do red for work, blue for my kid, yellow for things like doctor's appointments, and green for my social life) or color-code your class subjects like we used to do with ringed notebooks.

Pilot Metropolitan Fountain Pen for $34: I never understood the appeal of a fountain pen until I bought one. A properly smoothed fountain pen nib requires very little pressure to write with and seems to glide across the page with a soft, satisfying scratching sound. I know, I'm one of those people now. Much of my initial skepticism came from the perceived complexity of caring for and using a fountain pen, which is very much overblown. My favorite pen of the dozen I've tested is the Pilot Metropolitan with the fine nib. It's easy to work with, taking either prefilled ink cartridges, which you can pop in and out without ever spilling any ink, or you can fill it yourself using a converter and the ink of your choice. I started off using the cartridges, but eventually my quest for a waterproof ink led me to the converter and this sketching ink. Once a week or so, I dip the Metropolitan nib in the bottle of ink and twist the converter to fill the chamber with ink—that's all there is to it. Whichever fountain pen you find works best for you, you’ll find you'll have a quite simply better writing experience. —Scott Gilbertson

Plum Paper Seasonal Stickers for $10: There are a lot of stickers out there you could use for your planners, but my favorites—especially for the holidays—are from Plum Paper. They're beautiful and fun, and are mostly nice and small to fit into small lines or monthly charts without eating up the entire section. I like that there's a mix of shapes and styles, and you can also shop stickers for themes like home, fitness, wellness, and baby milestones. You can even make your own custom stickers (starting at $12), which are only thick line-style stickers where you can customize the word and icon on them. Still, very handy!

Not everyone needs or wants a rigid planner. If you just need daily to-do lists or are a fan of bullet journals, consider getting a great notebook instead.

Maybe you just want a plain, lined notebook. One of our former reviewers recommended the Midori MD Notebook, and I found it to be a nice small size if you're looking for something minimal. It comes in lined, unlined, or dot-grid, and uses paper made from cotton pulp (just like money!) Midori’s notebooks are designed to fit inside notebook or journal covers (which you can find all over Etsy). The pages are a subtle off-white and have a weight and texture that draw you in.

One of our reviewers skips a planner entirely and instead writes down his to-do list on a 3-by-5 index card. He puts that index card into his pocket with a pocket-sized memo book like this one from Field Notes ($13 for three), where he jots down notes throughout the day to use for the next day's to-do list. Both the notebook and index cards fit inside a waxed canvas notebook cover to keep them safe from the elements (or just his pocket). It's an affordable and easy-to-manage system.

Studies show that it's good for your brain to write things down. Sure, you could put your calendar in an online tool, but putting pen to paper activates more brain connectivity. We're more likely to remember and learn things if we write them down by hand, so using a paper planner for your to-do list can make it easier to remember. Plus, it's fun! You're given a creative space to let out everything you need to remember, from appointments to the day's tasks, and customize it in a way that best helps you stay organized.

What Style Paper Planner Is Best for You?

Paper planners mainly come in two styles: weekly and daily. Daily planners have an entire page dedicated to each day, while weekly planners have an entire week spread across just two pages. These aren't the only options (monthly is another popular one, for example, but not as popular as these two styles), but they're the most common you'll see. I like daily planners for folks who have a really busy schedule they want to plan out, and long daily to-do lists. Weekly planners are great if you want to be able to write down a few things per day but don't need an entire page.

Here are a couple common planner sizes. My favorite are the larger sizes since I like lots of room to doodle, but the smaller A5 is a popular choice for a book-sized planner that won't take up too much space. Not all paper planners use the same sizing names—Moleskine, for example, calls its A5 size a large—so you'll want to check measurements before you purchase.

#685. Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression

A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize. Researchers at the University of Missouri have found that older adults who follow regular daily schedules tend to experience less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggle to get a good night's sleep.

The findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an important role in physical and mental well-being. By helping the body maintain its natural internal clock, a predictable routine could offer health benefits that extend beyond improved sleep.

The discovery could be especially important for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties. According to the National Council on Aging, roughly half of adults age 60 and older report symptoms of insomnia, a condition that can make it difficult to fall asleep, stay asleep, or get restful sleep.

Daily Routines Linked to Less Pain and Depression

To investigate the relationship between sleep, daily habits, and overall health, Eunjin Tracy, an assistant professor in the College of Education and Human Development at the University of Missouri, examined survey responses from 67 older adults. Among the participants, 37 reported experiencing insomnia.

As researchers expected, those with insomnia generally reported more physical pain and higher levels of depression than participants without the condition. However, another pattern emerged when Tracy examined their daily routines.

Participants who maintained more consistent schedules tended to report less pain and fewer depressive symptoms, regardless of their sleep quality. This suggests that keeping regular daily habits may be associated with better health even when sleep problems persist.

"Regardless of sleep quality, those who reported having a regular daily routine had lower levels of physical pain and less depression compared to those without a daily routine," Tracy said. "If we are consistent with when we wake up, eat, work or study, interact with others and go to bed, those time cues help synchronize our internal body clocks. Over the long term, that seems to be linked with improved health outcomes."

One possible explanation involves the circadian rhythm, the body's natural 24-hour timing system. This internal clock helps coordinate when we feel awake or sleepy and influences numerous biological processes, including hormone activity, metabolism, and mood.

Rather than operating independently of our surroundings, the circadian system responds to signals that help it keep time. Light and darkness are especially important, but regular activities such as eating, working, interacting with others, and sleeping can also provide timing cues.

When these signals follow a predictable pattern, they help keep the body's biological rhythms aligned. Irregular schedules, on the other hand, can interfere with that coordination.

"When we regulate our circadian rhythm well, our bodies function well, but if it gets too distracted, our bodies don't function as well," Tracy said.

Although the study did not establish that regular routines directly reduce pain or depression, the findings point to circadian regulation as one possible explanation for the connection.

Even relatively small changes in daily schedules may disrupt the body's internal clock. One common example is social jet lag, which occurs when a person's sleep schedule shifts between workdays and days off.

Someone who wakes up early throughout the week but stays up late and sleeps in on weekends may experience this mismatch. The resulting disruption resembles some of the effects of traveling across time zones, even though the person has never left home.

Tracy suggests that maintaining reasonably consistent schedules throughout the entire week, including weekends, may help limit these disruptions and support healthier circadian rhythms.

"As someone who wakes up and goes to bed at the same time every day, I think a daily routine can be helpful for people of all ages across their lifespan," Tracy said. "There is growing awareness about the concept of social jet lag -- waking up and going to bed at different times on weekends compared to weekdays -- and the disruptions it causes to our circadian rhythm, so hopefully this research helps more people consider the health benefits of a daily routine. Since one-third of our lives will be spent sleeping, I think health and well-being research should be looked at holistically from a 24-hour perspective and not just focus on when we are awake."

A Simple Habit With Potential Health Benefits

The research highlights an aspect of healthy living that can be easy to overlook. While getting enough quality sleep remains important, the consistency of activities throughout the day may also be connected to how people feel physically and emotionally.

Because the study relied on survey data from a relatively small group of older adults, it cannot prove that adopting a regular routine will relieve pain or depression. Larger studies would be needed to establish whether changing daily schedules directly improves these outcomes.

Still, the findings suggest that a predictable daily routine may be a useful component of a broader approach to health, particularly for people experiencing insomnia.

For older adults and potentially people of other ages, simple habits such as maintaining regular waking times, eating meals on a consistent schedule, and limiting major changes in weekend sleep patterns may help support the body's natural rhythms.

The study, "Behavioral-social rhythms and insomnia symptoms: associations with pain, body mass index, and depressive symptoms among older adults," was published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine.

#684. Best Apple 3-in-1 Travel Chargers (2026): Anker, ESR, Satechi

A three-in-one travel charger that can power up my iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods is one of the first items I pack for any trip. I’ve tried out plenty of options, but these are my favorite chargers for keeping the holy trinity of Apple gadgets going strong while on vacation or a work trip.

Many of these picks will also happily charge Qi2 Android phones and other devices that support wireless charging. Since space is at a premium when traveling, they all feature clever compact designs. I’ve also included two-in-one options if you want to travel even lighter.

If you want something for your desk or nightstand when you’re back home, check out our Best Apple 3-in-1 Wireless Charging Stations and Best Wireless Chargers guides, and for power on the go, read our Best Travel Adapters, Best Power Banks, and Best MagSafe Power Banks guides.

Updated November 2026: I added chargers from Peak Design and Mophie, removed some older devices, and updated links and prices.

A classy look elevates this folding three-in-one stand charger, which accommodates your phone in portrait or landscape orientation. It is Qi2 25W-certified, so it can deliver 25 watts to supported phones (15 watts to others). There’s a fold-out Apple Watch charger on the back to fast-charge Apple Watch (Series 7 and above), and a spot for earbuds on the base. It feels sturdy and secure, with rubber grips to prevent sliding, and supports StandBy mode. It’s relatively compact for travel, but also looks good enough to be your permanent bedside charger. Not only does the whole thing fold flat, but it also comes with UK and EU adapters for the included power brick.

Satechi’s latest model is plastic with a soft-touch finish; the original version ($130) was more luxurious, with vegan leather and aluminum. The original is still a great option if you don’t mind the 15-watt charging rate.

Packing space is often limited when you travel, so it’s very handy that Anker’s MagGo folds down to a slim, compact form. Despite the small size, it packs plenty of power, charging your iPhone or Qi2-certified phone at up to 15 watts on a magnetic pad that you can adjust to your preferred angle. A second pad behind the main one charges AirPods or other wireless earbuds, and there’s a fold-out Apple Watch charger.

It can feel a little crowded when fully loaded, but I appreciate the space-saving design when packing it in a bag. While you can find faster options with chargers that support Qi2 25W, they’re not widely available and make little difference if you charge your devices overnight.

This cute, compact charging kit comes in a soft faux-leather bag. Unzip it to find a folding charger with a tiltable pad for your iPhone, a pad underneath for your AirPods, and a pop-up Apple Watch charger to the side. It comes with a 5-foot USB-C cable and a power adapter with fold-out prongs and three plug attachments (EU, UK, and AU). Everything is color-matched in black or cream, unless you opt for the special edition in orange and teal.

ESR’s folding charger delivers 25-watt charging for Qi2 25W-supported phones, fast Apple Watch charging, and an effective cooling fan. This three-in-one model folds away neatly and has a strong magnetic pad that supports portrait or landscape orientation. You can also adjust the angles for the phone and watch chargers. The fan is relatively quiet, but I prefer total silence at night, so I was pleased to find a button that turns it off for when you’re trying to sleep.

The plastic construction doesn’t feel premium, but it is lightweight, and the rubber feet do a decent job of preventing it from sliding around. It is more expensive than ESR’s previous release, the HaloLock, and the faster charging probably isn’t worth it if you’re primarily charging overnight, but overall it is a decent travel charger with a speed boost.

With a clean white finish, an elegant folding design, and warm ambient light, this Journey charger is a delightful travel companion. Ordinarily, I hate superfluous lights on a charger, but this isn’t a pointless LED; it’s a gentle glow from behind the Apple Watch shelf on the back, with a touch-sensitive power button on the front. It’s nice to have when you wake up in an unfamiliar, pitch-dark hotel room. You can fold it out to stand mode to charge all three Apple gadgets at once, or lay it flat if you just need to charge your iPhone and AirPods.

While this folding charger isn’t quite as compact as Anker’s below, I love that you can use the iPhone charging pad when it’s folded up. The Apple Watch charger can also pop up for Nightstand mode. It’s finished in a soft faux leather and folds flat for easy carrying in the included pouch. You get a cable to plug into the USB-C port, but no power supply, so you’ll need to provide a 30-watt power adapter. There is also a two-in-one version ($80) for just your iPhone and Apple Watch.

If you are really pressed for space, this is the smallest three-in-one charger you can get. It folds up to resemble a macaron and is easy to stow, but it’s not a power bank, so you do still need a cable and wall charger (both supplied). Unfolded, you get a magnetic pad to charge your iPhone at up to 15 watts, a middle pad for your AirPods, and an Apple Watch charger on the right. The design is lovely to handle, with a soft-touch finish and a durable silicone strap. I still prefer stand-style chargers because they allow you to angle your iPhone and use StandBy mode, but the MagGo UFO lets you travel as light as possible.

More stylish and compact than the other options listed here, this two-in-one charger from Peak Design folds flat for easy stowing. Open it to reveal a base with a channel for a USB-C cable and a Qi2 25W charging pad, plus a second swiveling Qi2 25W pad on top. You can charge two phones, or a phone and wireless earbuds. There’s also a USB-C port on the side, so you can plug in a third device, or a watch or ring charger. It comes with a cable, but you’ll need a power adapter (45-watt minimum). I like Peak Design’s 65W Dual Slim Charger ($65), but you don’t have to spend that much.

This genius petite gadget is perfect for folks who love to travel light. It’s an Apple Watch charger with a handy carabiner you can clip to your key ring or bag strap. Rotate the magnetic pad, and a USB-C jack pops out. Just to be clear, this is not a power bank—you must plug it into your MacBook, a USB-C port on a wall adapter, or even your iPhone to charge your Apple Watch. It doesn’t get more portable than this.

UAG SRGE 3-in-1 Travel and Desktop Charger for $100: This charger was close to earning a top spot until I saw the price (regularly $165). It’s a very smart charging kit that folds flat and comes in a snazzy zip-up bag with a 4-foot braided USB-C cable and a 25-watt power adapter, including plugs for the US, UK, and Europe. You can prop your iPhone at different angles on the MagSafe stand, and it works well with StandBy mode and Nightstand mode for your Apple Watch, but it’s not Qi2-certified, so you won’t get the stated 15-watt charging for an iPhone.

Mophie 3-in-1 Travel Charger With MagSafe for $150: This little travel kit is the older version of our pick above, but it’s still good (especially if you find it on sale). It also comes with a carrying case, charging brick, and USB-C cable. The square stack unfolds to reveal three wireless chargers in one elongated pad. The iPhone sticks magnetically to the center (15 watts), and the Apple Watch dock supports Nightstand mode. There’s also a grooved spot for the AirPods. It works well and is pretty lightweight and compact.

Twelve South Butterfly Travel 2-in-1 MagSafe Charger for $80: This uber-compact two-in-one charger looks like a hockey puck. Open the Butterfly, and you’ll find two pads attached with a rubbery silicone material. You can fast-charge an Apple Watch on one—even popping the charger up to take advantage of Nightstand mode—and the other circle lets you recharge your MagSafe iPhone at 15 watts. It’s a super compact solution, and Twelve South includes a 30-watt power source and cable with international plug adapters.

Native Union Voyage 2-in-1 MagSafe Charger for $100: For a slightly lower price, former WIRED reviews editor Adrienne So likes Native Union’s Qi2 butterfly solution, which doesn’t include plug adapters but comes in a tidy travel pouch and includes a cable.

Kuxiu Qi2 25W Travel Charging Station: This charger folds down to an impressively small package, and it feels sturdy with a silicone-covered metal construction. It can hit 25 watts for supported Qi2 25W phones, comes in a few different finishes, and ships with a 45-watt power adapter and USB-C cable in the box. Unfortunately, I don’t like how it looks, and I found it awkward to charge all three devices at once. It’s actually so compact that it feels crowded.

Mous Travel Charger: While the compact, folding design and low price impressed me, it gets kinda warm when you charge all three of your Apple devices, and the AirPods spot is finicky.

Most of my picks are MagSafe or Qi2-certified wireless chargers. That means they take advantage of the magnets embedded in the back of the iPhone 12, iPhone 13, iPhone 14, iPhone 15, iPhone 16, iPhone 17, and iPhone 18 ranges. The magnets ensure perfect alignment, enabling faster and more efficient wireless charging.

Qi2 is a wireless charging standard that Apple worked with the Wireless Power Consortium to develop. Compared to the original Qi standard, it brings MagSafe-style magnetic charging, enabling faster charging rates and improved efficiency. Apple updated the iPhone 12 and newer to support Qi2, but it’s not just for Apple phones; other phones can get Qi2 certification. While Qi2 Android phones are still thin on the ground, you’ll find Qi2 in Google's Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 series, and there are Qi2-ready phones that add magnets via a compatible case.

Qi2 charging mostly goes up to 15 watts, but the Qi2.2 update, branded as Qi2 25W, goes up to 25 watts. Support for Qi2 25W is currently limited and includes the iPhone 17 and 18 range and the Pixel 10 Pro XL and Pixel 11 range.

If you use a case, make sure it is MagSafe- or Qi2-compatible. A normal case will weaken the pull of the magnets in the device and will not stick to chargers as well. If your case is too thick, your phone may not charge at all.

MagSafe is also available in the AirPods charging case (depending on your model). Apple’s AirPods and AirPods Pro with the wireless charging case work with nearly all standard Qi wireless charging pads (as do many third-party wireless earbuds), but if you have AirPods with MagSafe, you can also connect them to magnetic mounts.

I mention StandBy and Nightstand modes throughout this guide, but what are they?

StandBy mode was introduced in iOS 17. When you place your iPhone on a charger in landscape orientation, it turns the screen into a smart display to show the time (with different clock designs to choose from), photos from your library, or widgets. If your iPhone supports an always-on screen, you can set it to turn off automatically after a set time when the iPhone isn't in use or when the room is dark. Head to Settings > Standby to customize it.

Nightstand mode shows the time on your Apple Watch when it’s sitting upright and charging, so it can serve as a bedside clock. You can customize this on your Apple Watch by heading to Settings > General > Nightstand mode.

#682. A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly important role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections. Scientists at Rockefeller University have discovered that when the body runs low on arginine, a key part of its immune defense system can stop working properly, potentially allowing dangerous cells and viruses to escape detection.

Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods. It is essential for making proteins that perform countless functions throughout the body. Researchers have long known that unusually low arginine levels are associated with several diseases, including colon cancer, but exactly how this shortage affects the body's defenses has remained unclear.

Now, new research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats. In experiments involving mice, increasing dietary arginine reduced the formation of colon cancer tumors and lessened the severity of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 infections. Remarkably, providing arginine after mice had already contracted influenza also improved their outcomes.

The findings, published in the journal Cell, raise the possibility that an inexpensive, readily available supplement could eventually become a useful addition to cancer treatments and strategies for combating viral infections. However, further research in humans is needed to determine whether the benefits observed in mice translate into effective treatments for people.

How a Missing Nutrient Could Help Cancer Escape the Immune System

The research was led by Sohail Tavazoie, who directs the Elizabeth and Vincent Meyer Laboratory of Systems Cancer Biology at Rockefeller University. His team has spent years investigating how arginine influences cancer development and progression.

In 2023, the researchers discovered that depriving colon cancer cells of arginine caused them to accumulate more genetic mutations. These changes can contribute to the unpredictable behavior of cancer cells, raising important questions about how arginine shortages might influence the disease.

The latest study reveals another potentially significant consequence. When arginine becomes scarce, cells struggle to produce enough of a crucial immune system protein known as MHC-1. This protein acts as a warning system, helping immune cells identify potential dangers such as cancerous changes or viral infections.

Without enough MHC-1, abnormal or infected cells may become harder for the immune system to recognize.

Encouragingly, the researchers also found that supplying a moderate amount of arginine, comparable to the quantity available in a couple of over-the-counter supplement tablets, could help restore production of this important protein.

"Our work reveals how a lack of arginine interferes with the immune system, and suggests that upping arginine intake could prove beneficial," says first author Qiushuang Wu, a postdoc in the lab. "Perhaps that means it could be used in combination with other therapies to treat both cancer and viral infections."

"Arginine supplementation could be readily tested in patients receiving immunotherapies or given to high-risk populations exposed to viral pathogens," Tavazoie suggests. "Considering that arginine is inexpensive and readily available, we hope that therapeutic and preventative studies could be undertaken soon."

The Surprising Connection Between Arginine and Immune Defenses

To understand why arginine has such an important effect, the researchers investigated how cells use amino acids to manufacture proteins.

Proteins are built from amino acids according to genetic instructions encoded in DNA. These instructions are copied into messenger RNA, which carries the information to the cellular machinery responsible for protein production.

The instructions are read in groups of three genetic letters called codons. Each codon specifies an amino acid or provides another signal needed during protein production. Arginine is unusual in that six different codons can specify it, reflecting the multiple ways its incorporation into proteins can be encoded.

Scientists already knew that changes in amino acid availability could affect cellular metabolism and signaling, two processes that help regulate how cells obtain energy and respond to their surroundings. What remained less clear was whether shortages of particular amino acids could directly influence which proteins cells produce.

To investigate, Wu examined the effects of arginine availability across several disease models, including colon cancer, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2. Each of these diseases has previously been associated with abnormal levels of various amino acids.

The research was supported in part by the Stavros Niarchos Foundation (SNF) Institute for Global Infectious Disease Research at The Rockefeller University and the Weill Cancer East Hub.

"One of the most dramatic patterns to emerge was that arginine was the most depleted amino acid in all of these diseases," she says.

Why Low Arginine Levels Can Disrupt the Immune System

In laboratory experiments using cultured cells, Wu examined how arginine shortages affected protein production. She identified 414 proteins whose levels dropped abnormally when arginine was scarce.

Many of these proteins were associated with biological functions already known to depend on arginine. However, the researchers uncovered a more unexpected effect involving three genes from the HLA family.

These genes provide instructions for producing proteins associated with MHC-I (major histocompatibility complex class I), an essential component of the immune system's ability to recognize threats.

MHC-I proteins are displayed on the surfaces of cells throughout the body. They act somewhat like identification displays, presenting small fragments of proteins from inside the cell to immune cells known as T cells.

When these displays reveal suspicious material, such as proteins produced by a virus or abnormal proteins associated with cancer, T cells can recognize the danger and help coordinate an immune response.

But the researchers found that arginine deficiency interfered with the production of these molecular warning signals.

The reason involved ribosomes, the tiny cellular machines that assemble proteins by following genetic instructions. Because the proteins involved in MHC-I production require arginine at numerous points, the researchers suspected that an insufficient supply could interfere with their assembly.

Further experiments confirmed that suspicion. When arginine was unavailable, ribosomes stalled while trying to manufacture MHC-I proteins. Without enough of the required amino acid, the cells could not efficiently complete the process.

As a result, fewer MHC-I proteins reached the cell surface, reducing the signals that would normally alert T cells to cancer-associated or viral proteins. This created an opportunity for dangerous cells to avoid immune detection.

"These findings are exciting because they reveal that consumption of a specific amino acid can directly regulate gene expression in an organism by increasing production of a protein enriched in that amino acid," Tavazoie says. "We believe that such selective translational tuning of gene expression through dietary manipulation likely extends to many other proteins and amino acids."

More Arginine Meant Fewer Colon Cancer Tumors in Mice

After identifying the molecular mechanism, Wu investigated whether changing the amount of arginine in an animal's diet could influence disease outcomes.

Mice receiving diets low in arginine developed more colon cancer tumors. In contrast, mice consuming higher amounts of the amino acid developed fewer tumors.

These findings provided evidence that arginine availability can influence cancer development through its effects on the immune system, rather than simply changing how individual cancer cells behave.

The results also raised a broader question: If arginine helps immune cells recognize cancer, could it provide similar benefits when the body encounters dangerous viruses?

Arginine Also Improved Outcomes From Influenza and COVID-19 Viruses

To explore that possibility, Wu collaborated with Heinz-Heinrich Hoffman, a research assistant professor in Charles Rice's Laboratory of Virology and Infectious Disease.

Together, they examined the effects of dietary arginine in mouse models of influenza and SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19.

The findings followed the same general pattern seen in the colon cancer experiments. Mice consuming more arginine experienced less severe symptoms from viral infections, suggesting that adequate levels of the amino acid helped support the body's immune defenses.

The researchers then made an even more surprising discovery.

Arginine did not appear to be beneficial only when consumed before an infection. Giving mice additional arginine after they had already been infected with influenza also improved their outcomes.

"Not only did mice with an arginine-rich diet have milder symptoms from viral infections, giving the mice arginine after influenza infection improved their outcomes too," Wu notes. "That was very surprising. From our genetic models, we knew manipulating arginine levels had a strong effect on gene expression, but we didn't expect the dietary manipulation to be equally impactful."

The observation suggests that changing nutrient availability might influence how the immune system responds even after a viral infection has taken hold.

Could a Simple Supplement Improve Cancer and Virus Treatments?

The discovery has potentially important implications for understanding why some people become more vulnerable to cancer and severe viral infections.

Arginine levels naturally decline with age, and inadequate nutrition can further reduce the amount available to cells. The researchers suspect that these changes may contribute to the weakening of immune defenses seen in certain diseases and in older adults.

"Qiushuang's findings illuminate how poor diet and aging -- during which arginine levels naturally decline -- could create the perfect storm for the initiation of colon cancer. Similarly, age-related arginine loss could partially contribute to the greater mortality caused by respiratory viruses," Tavazoie says. "We're also investigating whether making dietary changes in other amino acids has beneficial effects in a variety of disease contexts. There are no doubt more discoveries to come."

The possibility of using arginine alongside existing cancer immunotherapies is particularly intriguing. These treatments work by helping the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. If low arginine levels interfere with the molecular signals required for that recognition, restoring the nutrient might help some treatments work more effectively.

The researchers also see potential for investigating arginine supplementation in people at elevated risk of respiratory viral infections.

For now, these possibilities remain experimental. The findings do not establish that taking arginine supplements prevents or treats cancer, influenza, or COVID-19 in humans.

Nevertheless, the research reveals an important connection between nutrition and immunity. Rather than simply providing the raw materials needed to build proteins, specific amino acids may help determine how effectively the body's immune defenses identify and respond to dangerous threats.

And because arginine is inexpensive and widely available, the discovery could provide a practical starting point for future studies aimed at strengthening the immune system against cancer and infectious diseases.

#680. Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess

Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang. Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes, investing in chips to train AI earlier than most.

But just as he’s leaving, the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia, where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great.

“Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says.

Already, competitors have started to move in.

Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026.

Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia.

Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models.

Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025.

And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes.

Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups.

In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale.

While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms.

Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere.

Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms.

Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says.

Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips.

Most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch.

Moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes.

But Moorhead says the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips.

But AI models are now so good at reading and writing code that they can port an AI model over to a competitor's silicon at speed.

Wafer, a startup that uses AI to port models to AMD and then serves them more cheaply, has seen revenue grow spectacularly in recent months, boasts CEO Emilio Andere.

Every time a major new open weight model is released Wafer can have it running on AMD hardware at least 80 percent as efficiently within hours, he says. Andere says AI is getting so capable that his engineers barely have to edit or review the code.

Dan Hutchinson, a veteran chip analyst, says Nvidia may be entering its “Intel swan moment,” referring to the 2019 replacement of engineering-focused CEO Brian Krzanich with its CFO Bob Swan. (Sound familiar? Krzanich also resigned after a relationship with an employee; Huang is alleged to have had multiple.) From there, the company’s focus shifted to sales more than technical progress. Bureaucracy ballooned and revenue tanked.

“Nvidia is now an Intel waiting to happen,” he says.

#679. A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study

An existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for new treatments for chronic neck and back pain. In experiments involving zebrafish, researchers found that the medication prevented abnormal mineral deposits from forming in the spine, a process that can cause spinal tissues to harden and vertebrae to fuse together.

The discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine. Researchers also identified changes in gene activity and metabolism that appear to contribute to this damage, revealing several possible targets for future treatments.

Although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer new ways to slow spinal degeneration. The research also demonstrates how zebrafish could help scientists investigate the causes of spinal disease and test potential therapies.

Most people experience back pain at some point in their lives, and one common cause is the deterioration of the spine's natural shock absorbers. These structures, called intervertebral discs, sit between the vertebrae and help the spine absorb pressure, distribute weight, and move comfortably.

Over time, the discs can lose their ability to cushion the spine, a condition known as intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD). As the discs deteriorate, they can contribute to pain, stiffness, and reduced mobility.

Despite the widespread impact and substantial economic burden of this condition, no medications are currently available that can stop or reverse the degenerative process. Surgery remains the only established long-term intervention for certain severe cases, creating an urgent need for treatments that address the underlying damage.

Researchers have long known that genetics influences the risk of developing spinal disc degeneration. One gene of particular interest is associated with collagen IX, a protein that helps maintain the structural integrity of spinal discs by supporting the network of fibers that holds them together. Variations affecting this gene have repeatedly been associated with disc problems that develop earlier in life.

To investigate how these genetic changes contribute to spinal damage, scientists at the Universities of Edinburgh and Bristol turned to zebrafish. They studied fish that had been bred without a functioning copy of the gene, allowing them to observe how its absence affected the spine as the animals grew older.

A Hidden Process Causes the Spine To Harden

The results revealed striking similarities between the genetically altered zebrafish and people with degenerative spinal disease.

As the fish aged, abnormal mineral deposits accumulated in the tissues separating their vertebrae. This process, known as mineralization, involves minerals collecting in tissues where they do not normally belong. In the spine, the buildup can cause normally flexible structures to become unusually rigid, much like unwanted bone forming in the wrong location.

The researchers also observed spinal fusion, in which neighboring vertebrae become joined together. Such changes can interfere with the spine's normal flexibility and movement.

Importantly, the scientists discovered that the damage began well before the mineral deposits appeared. An underlying layer that provides structural support during spinal development started to break down first, suggesting that deterioration of this protective framework may set the stage for later hardening.

This finding could help explain how genetic changes initiate a chain reaction that eventually damages the spine.

Surprising Links to Fat Metabolism and Vitamin A

To understand what was happening at the molecular level, the team examined patterns of gene activity in the zebrafish. This allowed them to identify biological processes that had become unusually active or disrupted as spinal degeneration developed.

The researchers found alterations in fat metabolism, the processes through which the body breaks down, stores, and uses fats. They also detected disturbances in a cellular signaling system called mTOR, which helps regulate cell growth, metabolism, and responses to nutrients.

Additional changes involved phosphate regulation and vitamin A signaling. Phosphate is an essential mineral involved in building bones and teeth, but its accumulation in the wrong tissues can contribute to abnormal hardening. Vitamin A signaling helps control how cells develop and function.

Together, these findings suggest that spinal disc degeneration involves more than the gradual wearing down of tissues. Changes in how cells process nutrients, regulate growth, and handle minerals may also play important roles.

An Osteoporosis Drug Blocks Spinal Mineral Buildup

One of the most promising discoveries came when researchers tested ways to reduce the spinal abnormalities.

A medication belonging to a class of drugs called bisphosphonates successfully blocked the abnormal mineral buildup in the zebrafish. Bisphosphonates are already used to treat osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker and more vulnerable to fractures. These medications help protect bones by slowing the processes that break down bone tissue.

The finding is especially intriguing because it suggests that a treatment already used in patients might also help researchers develop therapies for spinal degeneration.

The team identified other approaches that reduced spinal damage. Limiting how much food the zebrafish consumed led to fewer spinal fusions, as did medications that suppressed fat metabolism.

These results point toward fat metabolism and phosphate regulation as potentially important targets for future drugs.

However, the experiments were conducted in zebrafish, not humans. More research will be needed to determine whether the same biological mechanisms operate in people and whether targeting them can safely prevent or slow spinal disc degeneration. The dietary findings also do not establish that restricting food intake can prevent spinal damage in humans.

New Hope for Chronic Back Pain Treatments

The study was published in the journal Communications Biology and received support from Arthritis UK and BBSRC.

Dr. Erika Kague, who led the research at the University of Edinburgh's Institute of Genetics and Cancer, emphasized the potential significance of identifying treatments that target the underlying causes of spinal damage.

"For decades, surgery has been the only real answer for disc disease. By understanding the biology that drives the spine to harden, our zebrafish studies point to several ways of slowing it down, including a drug already used safely in patients. There's more work to do, but for a condition that's affected people for generations without a treatment in sight, this is super exciting."

The findings could be particularly important for the millions of people who live with persistent back pain and have limited options for preventing their condition from worsening.

Dr. Caroline Aylott, Head of Research Delivery at Arthritis UK, highlighted the potential benefits for patients.

"For the 9.5 million people across the UK living with back pain this research brings fresh hope that potential new therapeutic approaches are on the horizon.

"We are proud to fund research that is unlocking the science behind the processes leading to spinal disc degeneration. Back pain is one of the UK's most common conditions that has blighted millions over generations. Dr. Erika Kague and her team at the University of Edinburgh have uncovered important genetic evidence that could pave the way for new treatments, bringing us one step closer to a future where fewer people have to live with the daily pain and challenges that back pain can bring."

The research also illustrates the broader value of studying basic biological processes to understand diseases that affect large numbers of people.

Dr. Jef Grainger, Executive Director for Bioscience Advancing Knowledge at BBSRC, said:

"This research shows how publicly funded discovery bioscience can generate the knowledge needed to address major health challenges. By revealing new knowledge of how healthy biological processes break down in aging-related spinal disc degeneration, the study opens up promising avenues for future treatment development. It's a great example of how BBSRC-supported research helps turn scientific discovery into knowledge and innovations that have the potential to improve people's lives."

By identifying genetic and metabolic changes that contribute to spinal hardening, and demonstrating that some of the damage can be prevented in zebrafish, the researchers have opened several new avenues for investigating spinal disc degeneration.

For a condition that affects millions and has no approved drug capable of stopping its progression, these early findings offer an encouraging starting point for developing treatments that could one day protect the spine before serious damage occurs.
